title: Step Brothers
logline: Will Ferrell and John C. Reilly as fortysomething men-children forced to share a house. Escalating improvised absurdism.
subtitle_release: Step Brothers 2008 m-720p Roboris (fixed and corrected)
overview: Brennan Huff and Dale Doback might be grown men. But that doesn't stop them from living at home and turning into jealous, competitive stepbrothers when their single parents marry. Brennan's constant competition with Dale strains his mom's marriage to Dale's dad, leaving everyone to wonder whether they'll ever see eye to eye.

jokes.text: Brennan, a grown man, is watching TV at home as his mother leaves. 'Mom, I'm watching the thing with the lady.'
jokes.setup: Mom calls out to her son as she leaves the house — a normal domestic scene
jokes.punchline: His response ('I'm watching the thing with the lady') immediately establishes him as a child-brained adult who can't even articulate what show he's watching
jokes.explanation: Perfect character-establishing joke. 'The thing with the lady' tells us everything about Brennan in five words — vague, disengaged, childlike. High economy and character integration. Not quotable on its own but very effective as an opener.

jokes.text: Dale asks his departing father to leave money for pizza, then immediately asks 'But what if I want wings?'
jokes.setup: Robert leaves $20 for pizza, a reasonable parental gesture
jokes.punchline: Dale immediately pivots to demanding wings, treating $20 as insufficient — a grown man negotiating food money like a teenager
jokes.explanation: Mirrors joke #1 structurally — both men are introduced mid-childlike-dependency. Dale's negotiation over wings is funny because of the implicit power dynamic: a 40-year-old man wheedling over food money. 'You don't need wings' is a great dad-to-child line delivered to a full-grown adult.

jokes.text: Robert loses his train of thought mid-medical-presentation and says 'which eliminates the need to put your face between those breasts.'
jokes.setup: Robert is delivering a dry, technical medical conference speech about cochlear implants and external processors
jokes.punchline: He trails off with '...which eliminates the need to put your face between those breasts' — clearly distracted by a woman in the audience
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant: the deadpan technical language makes the punchline land harder. The juxtaposition of medical jargon with a completely inappropriate non-sequitur is well-constructed. Sets up Robert as a man who is about to blow up his professional life for a woman, which pays off immediately when he meets Nancy.

jokes.text: Robert says to Nancy, 'I'm sorry. I'm just... I'm so lost. And this never happens to me.'
jokes.setup: Robert just embarrassed himself by trailing off about breasts mid-presentation; now he approaches Nancy to introduce himself
jokes.punchline: 'This never happens to me' — a classic flustered excuse that's funny because we just watched it happen, and because it's the kind of thing someone says when it probably DOES happen to them
jokes.explanation: Functional callback. The irony that he just very publicly lost his composure makes 'this never happens to me' mildly funny. Not particularly original but earns its place by quickly closing the loop on the previous joke.

jokes.text: Robert introduces himself: 'My name is Robert, and I play racquetball. I collect coins.'
jokes.setup: Robert is trying to impress a woman he's clearly smitten with after a fumbled introduction
jokes.punchline: His self-description is catastrophically mundane — racquetball and coin collecting are the least seductive hobbies imaginable, delivered with apparent sincerity
jokes.explanation: The humor is in the gap between his romantic intentions and his spectacularly unromantic pitch. Coin collecting is a perfect detail — specific, unheroic, and slightly sad. The economy is excellent; two hobbies, perfectly chosen.

jokes.text: Nancy's rapid-fire self-introduction: 'I know how to make tandoori chicken, I contribute to NPR every single year, and I love the movies of Rob Reiner. Pilates changed my life.'
jokes.setup: Robert has given his sad little intro; Nancy fires back with her own
jokes.punchline: The list is a perfect satire of a certain kind of upper-middle-class self-definition — NPR, Rob Reiner films, Pilates — delivered at speed as if these are equivalent credentials
jokes.explanation: Sharp observational comedy about a certain demographic. Each item in the list escalates in comedy — NPR is relatable, Rob Reiner is specific, Pilates changed her life is the perfect absurd peak. Good character establishment in a short space.

jokes.text: Robert casually drops '...and I have a 40-year-old son, Dale, who still lives at home.' Nancy immediately: 'What did you just say?' Robert: 'I knew I shouldn't have told you that.'
jokes.setup: Robert is on a roll charming Nancy, listing attractive qualities (boat, travel plans)
jokes.punchline: He buries the admission that his 40-year-old son lives with him at the end of the attractive-qualities list, then immediately regrets it
jokes.explanation: Well-structured misdirection: the rhythm of the list lulls the audience and Nancy, making the Dale reveal a genuine surprise. 'I knew I shouldn't have told you that' is a great reactive punchline — self-aware and funny. The structure mirrors how the film will work: these adults trying to have adult relationships while burdened by their man-children.

jokes.text: Nancy immediately matches him: 'I have a 39-year-old son named Brennan who still lives at home with me.'
jokes.setup: Robert just confessed to Dale living at home, clearly expecting judgment
jokes.punchline: Nancy has the exact same situation — a 39-year-old man-child — perfectly mirroring his confession and immediately neutralizing the social awkwardness
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural mirror. The comedic payoff is entirely in the symmetry and the speed — she doesn't hesitate. It retroactively makes Robert's embarrassment funnier and sets up the entire film's premise in one line. High structure and economy scores are justified.

jokes.text: 'Get a room, Dad.' — Dale interrupting Robert and Nancy's wedding toast
jokes.setup: Robert is giving a warm, heartfelt wedding toast welcoming everyone
jokes.punchline: Dale shouts 'Get a room, Dad' — an absurdly inappropriate wedding-toast interruption that also reveals his hostility toward the relationship
jokes.explanation: The joke works more for what it reveals than for its originality. 'Get a room' is a cliché, but deploying it at a wedding toast at the groom is a specific character choice that tells us everything about Dale's maturity and possessiveness.

jokes.text: Robert explains Derek couldn't attend the wedding '...because of an important fishing trip.'
jokes.setup: Robert is excusing his youngest son's absence from his wedding.
jokes.punchline: The reason is a fishing trip — not an emergency, not a work obligation, just a recreational fishing trip that apparently outranked attending his father's wedding. Delivered by Robert with zero apparent irony.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the specificity of 'important fishing trip' and Robert's straight delivery of it. It quietly characterizes Derek as self-centered while also showing Robert's oblivious acceptance of the insult. Economical and effective.

jokes.text: Robert casually mentions Brennan 'was recently let go from his job at PetSmart' mid-toast
jokes.setup: Robert is giving a warm welcome speech at the wedding reception, mentioning that Brennan was going to move out
jokes.punchline: He adds the PetSmart detail as if it's a minor footnote, publicly humiliating Brennan in front of guests
jokes.explanation: The specific detail of PetSmart — not a prestigious employer to be fired from — is the key comic element. The casualness with which Robert drops this bombshell at a wedding is good cringe comedy. PetSmart as the punchline is a well-chosen specific detail.

jokes.text: Brennan erupts: 'I wasn't fired from my job, I was laid off! But you wouldn't know the difference. I didn't want salmon! I said it four times.'
jokes.setup: Robert just publicly announced Brennan was let go from PetSmart at the wedding
jokes.punchline: Brennan's defensive outburst escalates from defending his employment status to a completely non-sequitur salmon complaint, suggesting this wedding dinner has been going badly on multiple fronts
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The pivot from 'I was laid off!' — a defensible distinction — to 'I didn't want salmon! I said it four times!' is a masterclass in comic escalation and character revelation. The salmon complaint is completely non-sequitur, implying Brennan has been simmering about the fish throughout the entire ceremony and can no longer contain himself. The number 'four times' is a perfect specific detail. This is exactly the kind of improvised-feeling absurdist character comedy Adam McKay excels at. High marks across the board.

jokes.text: 'This wedding is horseshit.' — Brennan, presumably muttered from his seat
jokes.setup: Brennan has just had his salmon complaint and employment status dragged into the wedding toast
jokes.punchline: He punctuates it with this blunt verdict on the entire event
jokes.explanation: Five words that land hard after the salmon explosion. Its power is entirely in timing and economy — it's the period at the end of the outburst. 'Horseshit' is the right word choice: not 'terrible' or 'awful,' but the specific, childlike vulgarity of 'horseshit.'

jokes.text: Brennan in the car: 'I'm not gonna call him Dad.' Robert: 'Brennan, you're 39 years old. I would not expect you to call him Dad.' Brennan: 'Well, I'm not going to, ever. Even if there's a fire.'
jokes.setup: Brennan declares he won't call Robert 'Dad,' which Nancy reasonably agrees is unnecessary
jokes.punchline: 'Even if there's a fire' — the addendum implies a scenario where screaming 'Dad!' would summon help in an emergency, which Brennan pre-emptively refuses to do, revealing the depth of his petulance
jokes.explanation: One of the great jokes in the film. The setup is completely reasonable — Nancy agrees he doesn't need to call Robert 'Dad' — which makes Brennan's escalation to 'even if there's a fire' land like a thunderclap. The fire scenario implies he would rather burn to death than compromise his position. This is Brennan's character in a single absurdist line: petulant, theatrical, and self-destructively committed to his grievances. Genuinely original structure — the joke is entirely in the irrational escalation. Comparable in quality to the vasectomy anchor example.

jokes.text: 'Robert better not get in my face, because I'll drop that motherfucker.' Nancy: 'Jesus, Brennan.'
jokes.setup: Brennan has just said he won't call Robert 'Dad' even in a fire; now he escalates to physical threats
jokes.punchline: The threat of violence against a kind, mild-mannered doctor is absurd; Nancy's 'Jesus, Brennan' grounds it in reality
jokes.explanation: Good but slightly weaker after the exceptional 'fire' joke. The threat reads as performative bluster from someone who clearly cannot 'drop' anyone, which is the joke. Nancy's reaction is the straight-man punctuation. Functional character comedy.

jokes.text: Dale's list of 'what it means to be men': 'We like to shit with the door open. We talk about pussy. We go on riverboat-gambling trips. We make our own beef jerky.'
jokes.setup: Dale is arguing to his dad that he and Robert don't need women/change in their lives because they're men
jokes.punchline: The list of manly activities escalates from crude (door-open shitting) to mundane (beef jerky) with the riverboat gambling trip as a perfect absurd middle item
jokes.explanation: A great character-comedy list joke. The genius is in the specific mundanity of 'riverboat-gambling trips' and 'make our own beef jerky' — these are not rock-and-roll masculine activities, they're the pathetic fantasy of a man-child imagining adulthood. The escalation from toilet humor to this strangely pastoral vision of manhood is very funny. High character integration because only Dale would construct this particular vision of masculinity.

jokes.text: Robert flatly: 'We literally have never done any of those things.'
jokes.setup: Dale has just delivered his impassioned manifesto of masculine activities they do together
jokes.punchline: Robert's calm, complete deflation — 'literally never' — reveals the entire list was Dale's fantasy, not their actual life
jokes.explanation: Perfect straight-man punchline. The key comedic element is 'literally' — it's not 'we haven't done all of those,' it's categorical: none of it, ever. The economy is near-perfect: nine words that completely demolish Dale's entire worldview. This is the ideal deadpan understatement delivery and it makes joke #15 retroactively funnier.

jokes.text: Brennan asks where Robert went to medical school; Nancy says Northwestern and Johns Hopkins; Brennan says 'Is that good enough for you?' / 'No, it's not.'
jokes.setup: Brennan is questioning Robert's credentials as if he has standing to judge
jokes.punchline: He dismisses Northwestern and Johns Hopkins as insufficient — from a man who just lost his job at PetSmart
jokes.explanation: The joke lives in the ironic gap between Brennan's total lack of credentials and his confident academic snobbery. The flat 'No, it's not' is a good button.

jokes.text: 'I smoked pot with Johnny Hopkins.' Robert: 'You don't know anyone named Johnny Hopkins.' 'It was Johnny Hopkins and Sloan Kettering, and they were blazing that shit up every day.'
jokes.setup: Robert mentions Robert going to Northwestern and Johns Hopkins (the medical schools); Brennan tries to one-up with a name-drop
jokes.punchline: Brennan conflates 'Johns Hopkins' (the medical school/hospital) and 'Sloan Kettering' (another famous medical institution) into fake people named Johnny Hopkins and Sloan Kettering who were his drug buddies
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable jokes in the film. The wordplay is elegant: Brennan mishears or willfully reinterprets prestigious medical institution names as people. 'Johnny Hopkins' is a natural-sounding name, which is part of the joke. The escalation 'and they were blazing that shit up every day' sells it completely — Brennan is entirely committed to the fiction. The character integration is superb: Brennan is exactly the kind of person who would try to compete with medical credentials by fabricating drug-friend name-drops. This ranks near the top of the reel.

jokes.text: Brennan describes his hypothetical seduction scenario: 'I've got a luscious V of hair going from my chest pubes down to my ball-fro.'
jokes.setup: Brennan is constructing an elaborate hypothetical about Nancy being attracted to him in the shower
jokes.punchline: The invented anatomical terminology — 'chest pubes' and 'ball-fro' — is absurdly specific and deeply uncomfortable
jokes.explanation: 'Ball-fro' is an inspired coinage — specific, grotesque, and strangely self-confident. The invented vocabulary ('chest pubes,' 'ball-fro') elevates this above a simple crude joke into genuine character comedy: Brennan is describing himself as genuinely attractive using terms that are objectively repulsive. The commitment to the scenario is what makes it work.

jokes.text: Brennan: 'She takes one look at me, and she goes, "Oh my God. I've had the old bull, now I want the young calf."'
jokes.setup: Brennan is building toward the climax of his hypothetical seduction scenario
jokes.punchline: The 'old bull / young calf' metaphor is an oddly rustic, almost folksy way to describe sexual desire — the incongruity of cattle-farming language in this context is funny
jokes.explanation: The agricultural metaphor is the unexpected choice that makes this funny. It's specific enough to feel improvised and genuine. Part of a larger escalating sequence (jokes 18-20).

jokes.text: 'And she grabs me by the wiener.' Robert: 'Shut the fuck up!'
jokes.setup: Brennan has been building an increasingly inappropriate hypothetical about Robert's new wife seducing him
jokes.punchline: The blunt anatomical term 'wiener' (childlike vocabulary) followed by Robert's explosion — his composure finally shattering — is the payoff of the entire sequence
jokes.explanation: The punchline works on two levels: the word 'wiener' (after the elaborate metaphorical buildup) is funny in its bathos, and Robert's 'Shut the fuck up!' is the best possible reaction — he's been patient until this precise moment. The structure of the whole sequence (jokes 18-20) builds perfectly to this. Robert's reaction is the actual punchline.

jokes.text: Brennan refuses to get out of the car when they arrive at the new house. 'Come on, Brennan.' — 'I'm fine here.'
jokes.setup: They've arrived at the new home; everyone is getting out of the car
jokes.punchline: Brennan declares he's 'fine here,' staging a silent protest in the car like a child refusing to go into a restaurant
jokes.explanation: A quiet but effective visual comedy beat — the image of a 39-year-old man refusing to exit a car. Works as character reinforcement more than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Neighbor Don asks if he can come over and touch Nancy's face. 'Sure.' Robert: 'Thanks. Good luck, guys.'
jokes.setup: Neighbor Don pops over for a normal-seeming neighborly chat
jokes.punchline: 'Can I come over this afternoon and touch your face?' is a surreal, non-threatening-but-bizarre request delivered as if completely normal; Nancy's immediate 'Sure' makes it stranger
jokes.explanation: Pure absurdism — 'touch your face' is specifically chosen to be strange without being overtly sexual or threatening. Nancy's instant agreement and Robert's normalizing 'Thanks, good luck' make it stranger. Feels improvised in the best way. The dog named Cinnamon immediately following (with the aggressive heel commands) adds a visual comedic capper.

jokes.text: Robert repeatedly shouting 'Heel! Cinnamon! Cinnamon!' at his dog as the neighbor interaction ends
jokes.setup: Don has just made his bizarre face-touching request and is walking away with his dog
jokes.punchline: The dog's name 'Cinnamon' and Robert's escalating commands ('Heel! Cinnamon! Cinnamon!') suggest a complete failure to train what is probably a small or ridiculous-seeming dog
jokes.explanation: Minor joke. The name 'Cinnamon' for a dog Don is visibly struggling to control is a small absurdist detail. Gets a mild laugh, more as ambient texture than a fully-formed joke.

jokes.text: Dale asks Nancy to make him a grilled-cheese sandwich the moment she walks in. Robert immediately shuts it down: 'Dale just ate. He's testing you to see how much he can get away with.'
jokes.setup: Nancy and Robert arrive at the house; Dale greets Nancy
jokes.punchline: Robert's immediate psychological dissection of Dale's behavior — speaking about him as if he's a child being tested — is funny because it's entirely accurate and delivered in front of Dale
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Robert treating Dale's food request as a parenting challenge to be managed. Calling his adult son's behavior 'testing' is both accurate and deeply condescending in the most affectionate way. Good character dynamic established quickly.

jokes.text: Brennan: 'I'm Brennan.' Dale: 'I'm Dale. But you have to call me Dragon.' Brennan: 'You have to call me Nighthawk.'
jokes.setup: Brennan and Dale meet face-to-face for the first time — a tense, awkward introduction
jokes.punchline: Both immediately escalate their names to aggressive fantasy alter-egos, suggesting both have elaborate self-mythologies; the specificity of 'Dragon' and 'Nighthawk' is perfect
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy. In two exchanges, we learn everything about Brennan and Dale's shared psychology: neither can back down, both have elaborate fantasy identities, and they're immediately locked in a power struggle. 'Dragon' vs 'Nighthawk' — neither is tougher, both are equally childish. The mirroring structure is perfect. This is one of the best character-introduction jokes in the film.

jokes.text: Robert tells Brennan not to do something (implied visual reaction to Brennan's behavior at the dinner table) — 'Brennan. Please don't do that.'
jokes.setup: First dinner together; Brennan is doing something at the table we can infer is childish/inappropriate
jokes.punchline: Robert's weary 'Please don't do that' implies something visually absurd — likely a face, a food behavior, or a gesture — without specifying, leaving the audience to fill in the gap
jokes.explanation: In the film, this accompanies a visual gag (Brennan is likely doing something with his food or making faces). Without the visual, it reads as a minor reaction beat. High rewatch value because the visual context makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Robert tells Dale that's enough ketchup; Dale continues. Visual: Dale drenching his food in ketchup despite being told to stop.
jokes.setup: Robert is parenting Dale at the dinner table about condiment usage
jokes.punchline: Dale continues applying ketchup in defiance, treating it as a power struggle; the volume of ketchup is the visual joke
jokes.explanation: Functional visual comedy. The ketchup battle is a good metaphor for the whole film's power dynamics but isn't particularly original as a standalone joke. Works as part of the dinner-table texture.

jokes.text: Nancy introduces 'fancy sauce' to Dale. The secret recipe: 'It's ketchup and mayonnaise mixed together.'
jokes.setup: Nancy builds up 'fancy sauce' as something special that Brennan loves, implying a sophisticated condiment
jokes.punchline: 'It's ketchup and mayonnaise mixed together' — the deflation of the 'fancy' branding against the mundane reality of thousand island dressing essentially
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the gap between 'fancy sauce' (a child's precious named thing) and the revelation that it's just two condiments mixed. Good character work for Brennan — he has named his ketchup-mayo. The extended sequence around it (see #29) adds cringe value.

jokes.text: Dale finally gets fancy sauce, tries it, and reports: 'I don't like it. It smells weird.'
jokes.setup: Brennan has been hoarding and savoring the fancy sauce; Dale finally gets access to it
jokes.punchline: Dale's flat rejection — 'I don't like it. It smells weird.' — after all the drama is a perfect anti-climax
jokes.explanation: Perfect punctuation to the extended fancy sauce sequence. The whole standoff was for nothing — Dale doesn't even like it. 'It smells weird' is a great specific complaint about something that is literally just two condiments. High structure score because it perfectly caps the sequence. The deadpan delivery makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Brennan claims to have a green belt in kung fu. Dale: 'I don't believe in belts. There should be no ranking system for toughness. But one time I wrestled a giraffe to the ground with my bare hands.'
jokes.setup: Robert tries to find common ground by noting both men are into kung fu; Brennan produces a green belt as credentials
jokes.punchline: Dale rejects the entire concept of ranking systems (which sounds philosophical) but immediately counters with the obviously false claim of giraffe wrestling
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The pivot from 'I don't believe in ranking systems for toughness' — which sounds like an actual philosophy — to 'I wrestled a giraffe' is a perfect comedic reversal. The giraffe is specifically chosen: it's large, awkward, and implausible, but not impossible enough to be dismissed as a dragon. The specificity ('to the ground with my bare hands') is exactly right. Robert's immediate 'That's not true, Dale. Don't be ridiculous' is perfect straight-man support. This is among the reel's best jokes.

jokes.text: Robert: 'So, Dale, what have you been working on recently?' Dale: 'Well... I manage a baseball team.' Robert: 'Little League?' Dale: 'Fantasy league.'
jokes.setup: Robert sincerely asks Dale about his activities, clearly hoping for something adult and legitimate
jokes.punchline: The 'Little League'/'Fantasy league' exchange is a perfect two-step misdirection — Robert assumes the most charitable interpretation, and fantasy league is simultaneously funnier and sadder than even Little League would be
jokes.explanation: Structurally flawless micro-joke. Robert's 'Little League?' is itself the setup — it's already a low bar, suggesting Robert has calibrated his expectations of Dale. 'Fantasy league' is then the perfect subversion: it's even less real than Little League (no physical activity, no children benefiting). The pause before Dale answers adds to the effect. Economy is nearly perfect — four words carry enormous comedic and character weight. One of the tightest jokes in the reel.

jokes.text: Dale: 'Take a picture. It'll last longer.' — to Brennan, who is staring at him
jokes.setup: Brennan and Dale are having their first tense dinner; there's apparently sustained eye contact
jokes.punchline: Dale deploys a playground-tier comeback ('take a picture') as his chosen weapon in a staring contest between two 40-year-old men
jokes.explanation: Intentionally a bad joke — a playground cliché deployed by a 40-year-old is funny because of how low-caliber the insult is, but as a standalone joke, it's weak. The comedy is in character psychology (Dale reaches for the worst possible comeback), not in the wit of the line itself.

jokes.text: Brennan can't bring himself to call Robert by his first name: 'That's right, Mr. Doback.' Robert: 'Call me Robert.' Brennan: 'That's right, Robin.' Robert: 'Robert.' Brennan: 'Robin.'
jokes.setup: Robert invites Brennan to use his first name in a friendly gesture
jokes.punchline: Brennan keeps slightly mishearing or subtly changing 'Robert' to 'Robin,' refusing to fully comply while maintaining plausible deniability
jokes.explanation: Very funny passive-aggressive joke. The genius is in 'Robin' — it's close enough to 'Robert' to maintain deniability ('I'm trying!') but clearly deliberate sabotage. The repetition makes it better: by the third exchange, the audience realizes Brennan will never say 'Robert,' and that the slight name-mangle is Brennan's chosen form of micro-resistance. Perfect character integration — this is exactly how Brennan would fight this battle.

jokes.text: Nancy describes Brennan as 'a very gifted singer.' Brennan: 'I'm really, really good.' Robert: 'How good?' Brennan: 'I've been called the songbird of my generation by people who've heard me.'
jokes.setup: Nancy tries to find something positive about Brennan to share with Robert
jokes.punchline: 'I've been called the songbird of my generation by people who've heard me' — the qualifier 'by people who've heard me' is simultaneously an attempt to establish credibility and a de facto admission that the audience is small and probably consists of his mom
jokes.explanation: One of the great lines in the film. 'By people who've heard me' is a masterwork of self-undermining. It sounds like it's strengthening the claim (these are people with direct evidence!) but it immediately raises the question: how many people, and who are they? The phrasing is exactly what someone with zero self-awareness would say to sound credible. Perfect character integration: Brennan is enormously self-confident about a talent he has rarely shared and cannot prove. Comparable to the best quotes in the film.

jokes.text: Nancy reveals she has only heard Brennan sing twice in his life — 'I'm his mom, for example, I've only heard him sing twice.'
jokes.setup: Brennan has just claimed to be the songbird of his generation
jokes.punchline: His own mother, who has lived with him for 39 years, has heard him sing a total of twice — which immediately contextualizes the grandeur of his claim
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback that lands the previous joke's setup with more force. 'Twice' is the ideal number — not 'never' (which would suggest he can't sing at all), not 'occasionally' (which would be plausible). Twice, over 39 years. The word 'for example' implies the sample size is representative.

jokes.text: Dale improvises a crude song: 'If you wanna get down on these hairy balls / Why don't you jump right in? / It's a crotch party right up in here / Why don't you lick on this big joint?'
jokes.setup: Robert has revealed Brennan's singing as a unique talent he barely shares; Dale immediately co-opts this to sing an obscene song
jokes.punchline: Dale's immediate response to the conversation about Brennan's precious, guarded singing gift is to sing a lewd song about his genitals — demolishing the moment
jokes.explanation: The specific cruelty is in the timing — he's not just making a crude joke, he's weaponizing it against something Brennan clearly holds precious. The song itself is shock comedy, but it's the targeted deployment of it that earns the laugh. The parents' reactions ('Hey!' 'Stop it!') are good reaction beats.

jokes.text: 'I remember when I had my first beer.' — Nancy (or Robert) dismissing Dale's song, followed by Brennan: 'That's so funny, the last time I heard that I laughed so hard I fell off my dinosaur.'
jokes.setup: An adult delivers the classic 'I remember when I had my first beer' dismissal to Dale
jokes.punchline: Brennan one-ups with 'I laughed so hard I fell off my dinosaur' — a deliberately terrible comeback that's funny because of its archaism and because Brennan clearly finds it devastatingly witty
jokes.explanation: The 'fell off my dinosaur' comeback is intentionally a bad joke delivered with pride. The humor is in Brennan deploying something he clearly thinks is a killer line. It's a mid-tier joke that works mainly because of Brennan's self-satisfaction.

jokes.text: Robert explains the room-sharing situation: Brennan and Dale must share a room because Dale refuses to give up his 'office drum set.'
jokes.setup: Robert is explaining sleeping arrangements to the blended family
jokes.punchline: The reason Brennan can't have his own room is that Dale has an 'office drum set' — the juxtaposition of 'office' and 'drum set' implies a room entirely designed around Dale's arrested adolescence
jokes.explanation: 'Office drum set' is a funny concept — it's not a studio, not a practice space, but an office that also has a drum set. The implication is that Dale has colonized a room as an adult space and filled it with a teenage pursuit. Good character economy.

jokes.text: Brennan immediately demands Nancy provide fresh fruit and chocolate chips in his pancakes. 'Write it so you don't forget.'
jokes.setup: Robert is trying to manage the bedtime/moving-in situation; Brennan addresses Nancy as she's about to leave
jokes.punchline: 'Write it so you don't forget' — Brennan is dictating grocery requirements to his new stepmother with the confidence of a child giving orders, including an administrative follow-up
jokes.explanation: The 'write it so you don't forget' is the best part — Brennan is not just making requests, he's managing Nancy's task compliance. The specificity of 'fresh fruit and chocolate chips in pancakes' is good: not an outrageous demand, but specific enough to be controlling.

jokes.text: Brennan says 'Good night, Mom' to Nancy; Brennan says 'Good night, Mr. Doback' to Robert — deliberately not 'Robert' despite being corrected earlier.
jokes.setup: Everyone is saying good night; Robert gently tried to get Brennan to use first names earlier
jokes.punchline: Brennan reverts to 'Mr. Doback' — skipping the whole Robin/Robert gambit and going even more formal, while warmly calling Nancy 'Mom' (the ultimate manipulation)
jokes.explanation: Good callback. The contrast is the punchline: Brennan instantly adopts 'Mom' for Nancy (cementing his position) while snubbing Robert with the formal 'Mr. Doback.' It shows strategic rather than random childishness.

jokes.text: Dale's house rules include: 'If there's any foods that you like, I suggest you put your name on them, or they will be thrown out. By me.'
jokes.setup: Dale is laying down house rules for Brennan in his new room
jokes.punchline: 'By me' — the two-word addendum clarifies the threat is personal, not systemic. It's the clarification that makes it a flex.
jokes.explanation: 'By me' is a small but perfect sentence. It transforms a neutral rule into a personal threat. The pause before it is the structure that makes it land. Good economy.

jokes.text: Dale: 'House was built in 1825 by General Custer.'
jokes.setup: Dale is giving Brennan a tour/orientation of the house with authority
jokes.punchline: General Custer (who died at Little Bighorn in 1876, not a house builder, historically irrelevant to this house) is an absurdly wrong historical detail delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: Perfect absurdism delivered deadpan. 'General Custer' is both historically implausible (he was not an architect) and weirdly specific (why Custer?). The specificity of the wrong answer is what makes it funny — Dale has clearly invented this, but with enough confidence that it sounds like he actually believes it. Great economy.

jokes.text: Dale's sacred drum-set room speech: 'This is my office and my beat laboratory.' ... 'Don't ever, ever, ever touch my drum set.' Escalates to: 'I was at about six there. You don't wanna see me go to 10.'
jokes.setup: Dale shows Brennan his room and issues a warning about the drum set
jokes.punchline: The 'I was at about six there' self-assessment — Dale is rating his own anger on a scale — reveals a person who has an elaborate internal anger management mythology about himself that is completely uncalibrated
jokes.explanation: The 'beat laboratory' is funny on its own (a child's grandiose name for a hobby space), but the 1-to-10 anger scale is the main joke. Dale rating his own intimidation display like a Yelp review of his emotions is perfect man-child absurdism. The confidence with which he delivers 'You don't wanna see me go to 10' — having just delivered a mild warning speech — is the comedy.

jokes.text: Robert explaining why Dale never left: 'Well, Dale has always coasted off my accomplishments.' Dale left college his junior year because he wanted to join 'the family business.' — 'But you're a medical doctor.' — 'Believe me, I've told him that.'
jokes.setup: Nancy asks Robert why Dale never left home
jokes.punchline: 'But you're a medical doctor' / 'Believe me, I've told him that' — Dale tried to join a medical practice by claiming nepotism applies, apparently unaware that medicine requires qualifications
jokes.explanation: The two-line exchange is very tight. 'Believe me, I've told him that' implies that the conversation 'Dale, I am a doctor, you cannot just join my practice' has happened multiple times. The exhaustion in that line is good character work for Robert. 'It's all about who you know' as Dale's response to being told medicine requires qualifications is excellent off-screen joke.

jokes.text: Robert: 'He just always says, "It's all about who you know."' — Dale's philosophy for entering the medical profession without a degree.
jokes.setup: Robert has explained that Dale dropped out to join his medical practice.
jokes.punchline: Dale's strategy for becoming a doctor without going to medical school is 'it's all about who you know' — a networking philosophy spectacularly misapplied to a licensed profession.
jokes.explanation: A button on the previous joke. 'It's all about who you know' applied to medicine is funny because it's the kind of logic that sort of works in entertainment or business but is completely inapplicable to a profession requiring a license. Good character specificity for Dale.

jokes.text: Nancy's story: When Brennan was 17, he entered a talent show singing from a pirate musical. His brother Derek replaced the choir with football buddies who sang 'Brennan has a mangina.'
jokes.setup: Nancy is explaining why Brennan stopped singing — giving the backstory of his singing trauma
jokes.punchline: 'Brennan has a mangina' — the specific, childish brutality of this song, delivered as an earnest explanation by his mother, is simultaneously dark and absurd
jokes.explanation: The setup (talent show, pirate musical) is elaborate but earns its length. 'Mangina' is a perfectly chosen cruel middle-school insult — specific enough to have clearly happened, absurd enough to be funny in retrospect. The payoff to the whole 'songbird of his generation' joke thread.

jokes.text: Nancy's escalation: 'And I have to admit, for a little while, I sort of joined in as well.' [singing 'Brennan has a mangina']
jokes.setup: Nancy is sympathetically recounting Brennan's humiliation
jokes.punchline: His own mother joined the crowd singing 'Brennan has a mangina' — the ultimate maternal betrayal, delivered with casual admission
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation. The story has been building sympathy for Brennan, so the revelation that Nancy herself joined the mangina chorus is a genuine surprise that recontextualizes the entire anecdote. 'For a little while, I sort of joined in as well' — the hedging ('sort of,' 'for a little while') makes it funnier because Nancy doesn't fully own it. This is dark comedy at its best: a mother casually confessing to publicly mocking her son to a room of strangers. Among the strongest jokes in the reel.

jokes.text: Derek won the talent show by lip-synching 'Ice Ice Baby.' Robert: 'Oh, that's a great song.' Nancy: 'It is.'
jokes.setup: Nancy has just finished the story of Brennan's humiliation
jokes.punchline: Robert and Nancy's earnest agreement that 'Ice Ice Baby' is a great song — validating the brother who destroyed Brennan while the two parents bond over Vanilla Ice
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the story. After the genuine darkness of the mangina tale, the parents connecting over their shared appreciation of 'Ice Ice Baby' (completely ignoring the moral dimension of what just happened to Brennan) is both funny and revealing. Great economy — four words close the entire sequence.

jokes.text: Robert and Nancy both agree: 'Oh, that's a great song.' / 'It is.' — a brief mutual appreciation of Ice Ice Baby.
jokes.setup: Robert just mentioned Derek won with 'Ice Ice Baby.'
jokes.punchline: Both parents sincerely agree it's a great song — immediately after just finishing a story about their sons' emotional damage. Their shared musical taste is a tiny, beautiful character detail.
jokes.explanation: A small but well-executed button. The pivot from emotional backstory to casual music appreciation is funny, and their sincerity about Ice Ice Baby characterizes them as people whose taste was formed in a specific era. Good economy.

jokes.text: Night scene: Brennan in the dark says to Dale, 'I just want you to know I hate you. So does my dad.'
jokes.setup: First night sharing a room; both men are in bed in the dark
jokes.punchline: 'So does my dad' — adding his deceased/absent father as a co-signatory to the hatred is both petulant and poignant, suggesting Brennan has been composing this statement for some time
jokes.explanation: The 'So does my dad' addition is the joke. Brennan has presumably been workshopping this bedtime declaration, and his best effort includes recruiting his absent father as a witness. It's both childish and strangely touching. The deadpan darkness of the exchange ('Well, that's fine.' / 'Because guess what, I hate you too.') is great.

jokes.text: Dale's counter: 'And this house sucks ass.' Brennan: 'Well, the only reason you're living here is because me and my dad decided that your mom was really hot and maybe we should both bang her.'
jokes.setup: Both are trading declarations of hatred from their beds
jokes.punchline: Brennan escalates to claiming he and his dead/absent father conspired to 'bang' Dale's new stepmother — the specific absurdity of a 39-year-old scheming with his father about this, in the dark, is funny
jokes.explanation: Good escalation in the bedroom war. The specificity of 'we should both bang her' (a 39-year-old and his absent father as a tag team) is absurd. Sets up the 'retard' exchange and further escalation.

jokes.text: Brennan's counter: 'I hate you too. And this house sucks ass.'
jokes.setup: Dale has declared formal nighttime hatred.
jokes.punchline: Brennan's response matches the tone perfectly — 'I hate you too' (formal mirror) then adds 'and this house sucks ass' as a sweeping property critique, escalating the declaration into a broader grievance.
jokes.explanation: A solid mirror response. 'This house sucks ass' is a good escalation — it's not about Dale anymore, it's a broader verdict. Works better as part of the exchange than as a standalone.

jokes.text: 'And we'll put up with the retard in the meantime.' — 'Who's the retard?' — 'You.' — 'Hey, y'all don't say that. Shut up. You'll wake up my dad and get me grounded.'
jokes.setup: Brennan has just lobbed a crude insult; Dale responds
jokes.punchline: Brennan's retort to 'shut up' is 'You'll wake up my dad and get me grounded' — a 39-year-old man's primary fear in this conflict is being grounded by his father
jokes.explanation: The 'get me grounded' fear is the best part of this exchange — it confirms Brennan's psychological worldview is entirely that of a teenager. The slur ('retard') is the kind of thing these characters would say and reads as character revelation rather than a punchline in itself.

jokes.text: Dale: 'Shut up. You'll wake up my dad and get me grounded.'
jokes.setup: Dale has just delivered an aggressive speech threatening Brennan.
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals his biggest fear is being grounded by his dad — a 40-year-old man is worried about his father's disciplinary authority. 'Get me grounded' is perfect schoolboy language from an adult.
jokes.explanation: One of the most concise character jokes in the reel. Dale has just been extremely aggressive and threatening, but the reveal that he's afraid of being 'grounded' is a perfect deflation. It simultaneously shows his bravado is performance and his actual power dynamics are those of a child.

jokes.text: 'You and your mom are hillbillies. This is a house of learned doctors.' — Dale. Brennan: 'You're not a doctor.' Dale: 'You're a big, fat, curly-headed fuck.'
jokes.setup: The bedroom insult war continues to escalate
jokes.punchline: 'This is a house of learned doctors' — Dale claiming academic prestige on behalf of his father, whom he has never medically assisted — followed by the immediate deflation 'You're not a doctor' and his response of 'You're a big, fat, curly-headed fuck'
jokes.explanation: 'You're a big, fat, curly-headed fuck' is a highly quotable insult because of its specificity. 'Curly-headed' is not a standard insult category — it's what you get when someone is reaching for something specific and lands on a physical description. The escalation from 'house of learned doctors' (pretentious) to 'curly-headed fuck' (completely artless) in two beats is good structure.

jokes.text: Dale: 'You better not go to sleep. As soon as your eyes shut, I'm gonna punch you square in the face.' Brennan: 'I hope you stay still when you sleep, because I'm putting a rat trap between your legs.'
jokes.setup: The insult war has escalated to threats
jokes.punchline: Both men have detailed, premeditated plans for violence against a sleeping person — the specificity of 'square in the face' and 'rat trap between your legs' suggests they've thought about this
jokes.explanation: The 'rat trap between your legs' is a great specific threat — it's not 'I'll hurt you,' it's a carefully considered genital trap. 'Square in the face' is also a good detail — 'square' implies precision, as if Dale has considered the optimal face-punch geometry.

jokes.text: Dale repeats back: 'I'm a curly-headed fuck?' — in a tone that is somehow both offended and genuinely processing the new identity label.
jokes.setup: Brennan has just called Dale a 'big, fat, curly-headed fuck.'
jokes.punchline: Dale's repetition of the insult as a question — 'I'm a curly-headed fuck?' — plays as genuine self-examination rather than pure anger. He seems to be weighing whether this is an accurate description.
jokes.explanation: A beat that works because of John C. Reilly's implied delivery. The question isn't just 'are you insulting me?' — it's 'is this my new name?' The existential weight Dale gives to the insult is funny.

jokes.text: Brennan: 'I'm gonna take a pillowcase and fill it full of bars of soap and beat the shit out of you.'
jokes.setup: The threat exchange continues to escalate
jokes.punchline: The soap-in-a-pillowcase threat is a specific piece of prison/military folklore (a 'blanket party') that Brennan has apparently researched — the specificity suggests genuine premeditation
jokes.explanation: The soap-pillowcase threat is funny because it's a real technique (from Full Metal Jacket, prison culture) being deployed in a suburban bedroom dispute by a 39-year-old. The gap between the seriousness of the method and the pettiness of the conflict is the joke.

jokes.text: Brennan: 'This is my house now.' Dale: 'How do you like The Gilded Lady?' — cutting to Robert and Nancy looking at their sailboat.
jokes.setup: The bedroom war has ended with Brennan declaring dominance; then we cut to the parents
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition: in the bedroom, two men are claiming ownership of the house; simultaneously the actual owners are dreaming about escaping on a sailboat called 'The Gilded Lady'
jokes.explanation: The structural irony — children fighting over house ownership while parents plan escape — is the joke. 'The Gilded Lady' as a name for the escape plan is a nice touch. The juxtaposition is good filmmaking and mild comedy.

jokes.text: Brennan: 'This is my house now.' — after Dale tells him to get out.
jokes.setup: Dale has demanded Brennan get out of 'my fucking house.'
jokes.punchline: Brennan's flat counter-claim — 'This is my house now' — delivered presumably with total conviction, is the perfect symmetrical response. It's both obviously untrue and stated as settled fact.
jokes.explanation: Five words, maximum economy, complete conviction. The humor is in the baselessness of the claim — Brennan moved in this afternoon and has already declared ownership. Works well as a beat in the escalating bedroom argument.

jokes.text: Robert stumbles into the pool/cold water: 'Oh, God! It's cold! Hey! Is anyone listening? Help!'
jokes.setup: Robert and Nancy are admiring the boat; the scene appears to be romantic and peaceful
jokes.punchline: Robert falls into the water — the physical comedy of the dignified doctor immediately in distress, calling for help over what is presumably a cold pool, while Nancy is right there
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy button to the reel. 'Is anyone listening? Help!' over a cold pool dip is mild slapstick — Robert's overreaction to cold water is in character for someone who just admitted he never does manly things. Not particularly original but serviceable as a final beat.

jokes.text: Dale sweating because he was 'watching Cops' — a transparently false alibi for touching the drum set
jokes.setup: Brennan asks why Dale is so sweaty, implying guilt about something
jokes.punchline: Dale's excuse — watching Cops — is immediately undermined by the later reveal that Cops doesn't start until 4
jokes.explanation: Works as a plant — the sweaty excuse is funny on its face (a 40-year-old getting sweaty from TV) but gains retroactive value when Brennan catches the alibi hole. Good structural planting.

jokes.text: Dale interrogates Brennan about the drum set with dead-serious detective energy: 'It's just weird... because seems like someone definitely touched my drum set.'
jokes.setup: Dale approaches Brennan with ominous calm about his drums
jokes.punchline: The gravity of a detective-level interrogation applied to whether someone touched a drum set — the mismatch of seriousness and triviality
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Dale's total commitment to treating a drum set like a crime scene. The understatement ('seems like someone') against the obvious rage beneath it is well-played. Strong character work.

jokes.text: Brennan maintains innocence with identical calm: 'Yeah, that is weird. Because I didn't touch them.'
jokes.setup: Dale's paranoid accusation demands a reaction
jokes.punchline: Brennan matches Dale's faux-calm tone perfectly, mirroring the absurdity back — clearly guilty
jokes.explanation: Functional comedic mirroring. The matching of Dale's energy by Brennan is funny but fairly standard straight-face denial comedy.

jokes.text: Dale's forensic evidence: 'I know you touched my drumstick, because the left one has a chip in it.'
jokes.setup: Dale has been building paranoid suspicion
jokes.punchline: He has CSI-level specificity about a drumstick chip, as if this proves anything about who touched it
jokes.explanation: The chip-in-the-drumstick detail is a perfect absurdist escalation — Dale has catalogued his drums like a detective catalogues evidence. Deeply character-specific to a man-child who treats his toys as sacred.

jokes.text: Brennan's psychological assessment: 'You sound insane, do you realize that? You should be medicated.'
jokes.setup: Dale has escalated to aggressive interrogation over drums
jokes.punchline: Brennan — himself a 40-year-old man-child living with his parents — diagnoses Dale as the crazy one
jokes.explanation: Good irony — the pot calling the kettle crazy. Works because both characters have zero self-awareness. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Brennan's alibi collapses: 'That's because you fucking touched my drum set... because I know Cops doesn't start till 4.'
jokes.setup: Dale sweated from 'watching Cops'; the alibi has been hanging in the air
jokes.punchline: Dale calmly destroys the alibi with TV schedule knowledge, paying off the earlier setup
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional structural comedy. The Cops schedule callback is the payoff to a plant established two minutes earlier. The specificity — that Dale knows exactly when Cops airs — tells us everything about these characters. It's a classic detective-reveal structure applied to the most trivial possible stakes. The earned callback elevates both jokes.

jokes.text: Brennan announces his retaliation: 'I'm gonna put my nut sack on your drum set.'
jokes.setup: The argument has been escalating; Brennan needs a nuclear option
jokes.punchline: The specific chosen act of desecration — teabagging a drum set — is both absurd and perfectly calibrated to hurt Dale most
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'you touched it' to 'I will teabag your sacred object' is the perfect man-child war escalation. The specificity of the threat and the matter-of-fact delivery make it land hard.

jokes.text: Dale's counter-threat: 'If you touch my drums, I will stab you in the neck with a knife!'
jokes.setup: Brennan has threatened to teabag the drums
jokes.punchline: Dale escalates from property dispute to murder threat with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The throat-stab threat is funny for its disproportionate violence but it's also slightly predictable — the 'man threatens to kill over trivial thing' beat. Reilly's delivery is what saves it.

jokes.text: Visual gag: Dale carefully and methodically teabagging every surface of the drum set while Brennan watches in horror
jokes.setup: Brennan threatened it; Dale swore death if it happened
jokes.punchline: The act is committed with such thoroughness ('Don't wanna miss a spot') that it becomes a performance piece
jokes.explanation: The visual payoff of the threat is a high-impact physical comedy moment. 'Don't wanna miss a spot' as a line of focus during the act elevates it from pure gross-out to character comedy — Brennan is meticulous about this desecration. The horror of Brennan watching is the reaction beat that completes it.

jokes.text: Dale attacks Brennan; in the ensuing brawl, Dale shouts 'I'm pre-diabetic!'
jokes.setup: An all-out brawl between two 40-year-olds is unfolding
jokes.punchline: In the middle of screaming threats, Dale randomly announces a medical condition as if it's relevant to the fight
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the film. Mid-brawl medical disclosure is both completely absurdist and deeply character-specific — only a 40-year-old man-child would think his pre-diabetes is tactically relevant information during a fistfight. Its complete randomness and Reilly's total commitment make it a quotable classic. The economy is perfect: three words that say everything about Dale. This approaches the 8+ anchor threshold.

jokes.text: "I'm pre-diabetic!"
jokes.setup: An all-out brawl has erupted; characters are fighting violently
jokes.punchline: In the middle of the physical altercation, Brennan screams a medical condition — completely non-sequitur, possibly as a plea for mercy or just panicked oversharing
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum impact. The complete irrelevance of a pre-diabetes disclosure in the middle of a violent brawl is a perfect absurdist non-sequitur. It's also deeply character-specific — Brennan is exactly the kind of man-child who would blurt out a minor medical condition during a fight as if it explains everything or should stop it. Highly quotable, nearly iconic. Approaches the 8.5+ tier.

jokes.text: 'You fucking fucker! I'm gonna rub my balls on your mom's face!'
jokes.setup: The fight continues to escalate
jokes.punchline: The insult 'you fucking fucker' is so incoherent it becomes funny, followed by an even more absurd threat involving the other character's mom
jokes.explanation: 'You fucking fucker' as an insult is funny for its impotent rage tautology. The mom threat is a callback to the schoolyard escalation pattern. The combination works but isn't especially novel.

jokes.text: Exchange: 'Your drum set's a whore! I teabagged your fucking drum set!' / 'Well, my drum set's a guy, so that makes you gay, you fucker!'
jokes.setup: Both are hurling insults mid-brawl
jokes.punchline: Dale's logical counter-argument — that because his drum set is male, the teabagging makes Brennan gay — is a schoolyard syllogism delivered with complete conviction
jokes.explanation: The 'my drum set is male therefore you're gay' callback is a brilliant piece of man-child logic — Dale has assigned his drum set a gender and uses it to win the insult war. It's both a callback and a perfect character moment: Dale treats the drums as a living entity with a sex.

jokes.text: During the brawl, Brennan shouts 'Rape! Rape! Rape!' repeatedly
jokes.setup: Physical fight between two men; someone is trying to stop it
jokes.punchline: Brennan's terror-cry of 'rape' in the context of a fight between two adult men is a grotesquely disproportionate response
jokes.explanation: Funny for the sheer panic and disproportionality — a grown man screaming rape during a sibling fight. Gets paid off later in the dinner scene, adding retroactive value.

jokes.text: Robert's colleagues overhear him frantically calling home about the fight, forcing him to summarize: 'There seems to be some savage fight going on between my son and stepson'
jokes.setup: Robert is at work, clearly mortified, trying to handle a crisis call professionally
jokes.punchline: The clinical understatement 'savage fight' while his wife screams in the background, observed by colleagues who clearly heard everything
jokes.explanation: The cringe of a professional man having to handle his children-men's chaos at work. The gap between his dignified demeanor and the chaos is the joke. Functional but not special.

jokes.text: "My mom is being eaten by a dog, there's nothing I can do!" — Robert on the phone while his wife describes the fight
jokes.setup: Robert is at work taking a call about the chaos at home
jokes.punchline: What Nancy actually says on the phone is garbled/interpreted by Robert as 'being eaten by a dog' — his baffled paraphrase of her hysteria is funnier than any direct description
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist misunderstanding gag that works as a scene-transition joke. Not exceptional but adds comedic energy to the intercut.

jokes.text: Robert's colleague observes 'Family issues, huh?' and Robert responds: 'I don't believe in talking about people's personal lives behind their back.' Then immediately from off-screen: 'Rape! Rape! Rape!'
jokes.setup: Robert nobly deflects gossip about his family crisis
jokes.punchline: The 'Rape!' screams audible through the phone puncture his dignity perfectly
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic timing — the high-minded statement about privacy immediately undercut by the screamed 'Rape!' echoing from the phone. The juxtaposition is impeccably constructed. Economy is excellent: the deflation happens in a single sound effect.

jokes.text: Robert arrives home and surveys the damage: 'What the fucking fuck?'
jokes.setup: Robert, an authoritative doctor, arrives home to pure chaos
jokes.punchline: His profanity-doubling ('fucking fuck') signals that even his adult vocabulary has broken down in the face of his step-sons
jokes.explanation: The 'fucking fuck' construction is a great character moment for Robert — a dignified man who has had the dignity beaten out of him. Very quotable and well-timed.

jokes.text: Dale and Brennan, battered and panting, separately comment on each other mid-fight: 'Such power. It's raw power.' / 'What are you doing? It's Shark Week.'
jokes.setup: Parents try to break up the savage fight
jokes.punchline: The two combatants start offering commentary on each other's fighting AND one of them cites Shark Week as a reason to stop fighting — suggesting they both want to watch TV more than they want to fight
jokes.explanation: 'It's Shark Week' as a ceasefire condition is a perfect man-child detail — television scheduling has more weight than their conflict. The mutual admiration mid-fight ('such power') is a great absurdist touch suggesting they enjoy this.

jokes.text: Robert lays down the law; Dale protests: 'Dad, why are you talking to me like this? I'm your son.'
jokes.setup: Robert is furious and treating them like misbehaving children
jokes.punchline: Dale, a 40-year-old man, pulls the wounded-son card as if that excuses the behavior — which only highlights how profoundly infantile he is
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Dale's entitlement to gentler parenting despite being 40 is very on-brand. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Robert: 'Today I saw my own son use a bicycle as a weapon.'
jokes.setup: Robert is trying to explain why he won't give Dale special treatment anymore
jokes.punchline: The quiet devastation of 'bicycle as a weapon' — a specific, absurd detail delivered with parental exhaustion
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the bicycle detail and its deadpan delivery captures Robert's entire emotional journey. It's funny because it's so specific and so sad simultaneously.

jokes.text: Robert: 'You yelled rape at the top of your lungs.' / Brennan: 'Mom, I honestly thought I was gonna be raped for a second. He had the craziest look in his eyes.'
jokes.setup: Robert is listing the insane things that happened during the fight
jokes.punchline: Brennan sincerely defends his rape-cry with a completely earnest explanation, as if this is a reasonable position
jokes.explanation: Brennan's sincere fear of being raped by his stepbrother during a drumset dispute is a great character beat. The callback justification ('he had the craziest look in his eyes') builds on the earlier joke well.

jokes.text: 'And at one point he said, Let's get it on.' / 'That was about the fighting. I'm so not a raper.'
jokes.setup: Brennan has claimed fear of rape; Robert cites further evidence
jokes.punchline: Dale's defense — 'I'm so not a raper' — is both a denial and an inadvertent acknowledgment that this is an accusation worth addressing
jokes.explanation: 'I'm so not a raper' is a brilliantly specific denial — the casual modifier 'so not' applied to the word 'raper' (not even the standard 'rapist') is pitch-perfect Reilly improvisation. It's both absurd and completely in character for someone who would use 'Let's get it on' as a battle cry.

jokes.text: Robert and Nancy's punishment: 'No television for a week.' — Dale and Brennan react with absolute horror: 'What?!' / 'You're fucking high!'
jokes.setup: Robert threatens 'no choice' — implying something severe
jokes.punchline: The punishment is 'no TV for a week' — appropriate for children, grotesque for 40-year-olds, and treated by the men-children as if it's a death sentence
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of an appropriate child-punishment applied to 40-year-olds, combined with their genuine devastation, is a perfect encapsulation of the film's central joke. 'You're fucking high!' as a response to 'no TV' is both hilarious and character-perfect.

jokes.text: 'This house is a fucking prison! On planet Bullshit! In the galaxy of This Sucks Camel Dicks!'
jokes.setup: Dale and Brennan are reacting to the TV punishment
jokes.punchline: The cosmic escalation of the metaphor — from prison to planet to galaxy, each layer more absurd — culminating in 'camel dicks'
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film and a masterclass in comedic escalation. The structure is perfect: each step adds a new cosmic layer ('house' → 'planet' → 'galaxy') while also escalating the vulgarity. 'Camel dicks' as the endpoint is both surprising and inevitable. This is approaching the top anchor — it's a setpiece of escalating absurdist comedy that became a cultural touchstone for the film.

jokes.text: Robert and Nancy discover evidence of sleepwalking: Nancy's purse in the freezer, couch pillows in the oven
jokes.setup: Robert and Nancy return home to find the house has been further disturbed
jokes.punchline: The specific displaced objects — purse in freezer, pillows in oven — reveal that BOTH men are sleepwalking destructively, not just one
jokes.explanation: The sleepwalking gag works on two levels: the absurdity of the specific objects (purse in freezer is funnier than under the bed) and the revelation that both men are equally troubled. The escalation from 'one problem' to 'they're both insane' is well-structured.

jokes.text: Robert and Nancy find Dale and Brennan sleepwalking; Dale mutters: 'I'll kill you, Leonard Nimoy.'
jokes.setup: Dale is sleepwalking; parents observe
jokes.punchline: In his sleep, Dale's subconscious targets a specific celebrity with a death threat
jokes.explanation: Four words that are almost perfect absurdist comedy. The specificity of Leonard Nimoy (not a random celebrity — a nerdy, specific choice that tells us everything about Dale's inner world) combined with the death threat is brilliantly economical. This is the kind of detail that works on rewatch because you wonder what Dale's dream narrative is.

jokes.text: "My little brother's even a bigger asshole than you are." — Brennan's warning about Derek
jokes.setup: Robert mentions Brennan's brother is coming
jokes.punchline: Brennan's comparative insult positions Derek above Dale in the asshole hierarchy — establishing anticipation
jokes.explanation: Functional setup line for Derek's arrival. Not funny on its own but serves the narrative.

jokes.text: Derek brutally critiques his children's choir performance: 'Flat. It's so flat. I can't even... You don't even look good while you're singing.'
jokes.setup: Derek is apparently coaching his young children in singing
jokes.punchline: The critique 'you don't even look good while you're singing' is an absurdly vain metric applied to children — only someone as narcissistic as Derek would add appearance to vocal critique
jokes.explanation: Perfect character introduction for Derek. The appearance-critique of his own children singing immediately establishes him as a world-class narcissist. 'You don't even look good' as a musical criticism could only come from Derek — high character integration.

jokes.text: Derek announces his solo: 'Okay, I'm gonna save it with this solo.' Then sings in an absurdly high falsetto: 'I'm Derek / And I can sing high like this / And I can sing high'
jokes.setup: Derek has panned his children; now he will demonstrate how it should be done
jokes.punchline: His 'solo' is literally just his name and a description of what he's doing — the content-free narcissism of announcing you can sing high as the entirety of the performance
jokes.explanation: One of the best Derek moments in the film. The 'solo' is entirely self-referential — the lyrics are literally 'I'm Derek and I can sing high like this' — which is the most economical character joke possible. It demonstrates his narcissism, his self-delusion, AND his genuine weirdness simultaneously. Adam Scott's commitment to hitting those notes makes it land as physical comedy too.

jokes.text: Reaction beat: someone (likely Nancy or Robert) responds to the Derek falsetto with a horrified 'Jesus!'
jokes.setup: Derek has been singing his absurd falsetto solo
jokes.punchline: The single-word horror-reaction functions as the punchline to the Derek singing bit
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat that punctuates the Derek singing joke. The economy is perfect but it's doing the minimum — just confirming what we already felt.

jokes.text: Derek name-drops his celebrity fishing trip: 'Not just the Cubes... but we had Chris Daughtry, Jeff Probst, super-chef Bobby Flay.'
jokes.setup: Derek is explaining why he couldn't attend the wedding — he was fishing with Mark Cuban
jokes.punchline: The cascade of specific D-list celebrities ('the Cubes,' Chris Daughtry, Jeff Probst) as a flex reveals Derek's social world — these are the almost-famous people who validate him
jokes.explanation: The specific selection of celebrities is a character masterclass — Mark Cuban is legitimately famous, 'the Cubes' is a forced familiarity, but Chris Daughtry and Jeff Probst reveal Derek's true social tier. 'Super-chef Bobby Flay' adds the food TV guy as if that completes the pantheon. The list builds in the perfect order.

jokes.text: Robert gently corrects Dale for interrupting Derek's story; Dale asks: 'Are bonito fish big?'
jokes.setup: Derek is telling an impressive fishing story; everyone is enraptured; Dale interrupts
jokes.punchline: Dale's interruption is the most basic possible question — not a challenge, not a witty remark, just a simple size inquiry that completely deflates the narrative
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the gap between the importance everyone assigns Derek's story and the utter mundaneness of Dale's question. It's also character-perfect: Dale isn't being malicious, he genuinely wants to know about fish size, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Derek: 'I forget where my story was going. Damn it, Dale.'
jokes.setup: Dale has interrupted twice; everyone has repeatedly apologized on his behalf
jokes.punchline: Derek trails off — suggesting his story had no substance to begin with — before assigning blame to Dale
jokes.explanation: Good deflation joke — the story that everyone treated as precious apparently had no ending anyway. Dale is blamed for a narrative failure that wasn't his fault.

jokes.text: Robert fawns over Derek: 'Gang, don't be mad at Dale for ruining the story. And possibly the evening.'
jokes.setup: Derek has been magnanimously forgiving Dale; now the full passive-aggressive escalation arrives
jokes.punchline: The addition of 'and possibly the evening' is a perfectly calibrated passive-aggressive escalation — from one story to the whole evening
jokes.explanation: Derek's passive-aggressive 'forgiveness' is a great character beat — the graciousness is a performance that makes Dale look worse. 'And possibly the evening' is the perfect understated escalation.

jokes.text: Robert gushes to Derek: 'Guilty as charged with the stories.' / 'From across the room, I feel like we have a thing. You and me, man. You're my new stepdad.'
jokes.setup: Robert has been charmed by Derek all evening; this is the culmination
jokes.punchline: Robert — a grown man — tells his adult son's brother that he 'feels like we have a thing' and declares him his 'new stepdad,' completely inverting the family hierarchy
jokes.explanation: The 'you're my new stepdad' inversion is a great comedic payoff to the Derek-worship subplot. Robert is so thoroughly seduced by Derek's confidence that he's willing to subordinate himself. The cringe is real but not excessive.

jokes.text: Dale, watching Robert fawn over Derek: 'I never heard that laugh before.' / Brennan: 'Dad, why are you acting so weird?'
jokes.setup: Robert is completely transformed in Derek's presence
jokes.punchline: Dale and Brennan, united for once, observe their parent's transformation with confused betrayal — the men-children are jealous of a different adult getting parental attention
jokes.explanation: Good beat that shows Dale and Brennan's first moment of alliance — against the shared threat of Derek stealing their parent. 'I never heard that laugh before' is a quietly devastating detail.

jokes.text: Dale admits to Brennan: 'You're right about your brother. Total dick.' / 'You know what? I still hate you, but you got a pretty awesome collection of nudie mags.'
jokes.setup: Dale and Brennan have a moment of unexpected alliance over disliking Derek
jokes.punchline: Dale maintains the antagonism ('I still hate you') while pivoting to genuine admiration for the pornography collection — the reconciliation is mediated through dirty magazines
jokes.explanation: The 'I still hate you but...' construction is a perfect character beat for men who can't express positive feelings directly. The pivot to nudie mags as the basis for respect is perfectly in-character and funny.

jokes.text: Brennan describes his '70s, '80s, '90s porn magazine collection: 'It's like masturbating in a time machine.'
jokes.setup: Brennan explains he has vintage porn from across three decades
jokes.punchline: The metaphor 'masturbating in a time machine' — which reframes historical pornography as temporal tourism
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the film and in the film's broader comedic canon. The metaphor is perfectly constructed: the setup ('from the '70s, '80s and '90s') creates the temporal structure, and 'masturbating in a time machine' reframes the mundane act as science fiction adventure. It's original, economic (six words), character-perfect (only Brennan would think of this as a selling point), and structurally impeccable. This is a 9+ craft joke — genuinely exceptional.

jokes.text: Derek describes his real-estate motivation: 'you know what really gets my dick hard? Helping out my friends.'
jokes.setup: Derek is making a generous-sounding business offer
jokes.punchline: The pivot from business language to sexual arousal metaphor ('gets my dick hard') applied to friend-helping — the crass anatomy of Derek's bro-speak
jokes.explanation: Very character-specific for Derek — the bro who translates everything into sexual arousal metaphors. The juxtaposition of generosity and vulgarity is a good Derek beat.

jokes.text: "I got my real-estate license a few years back for shits and gigs."
jokes.setup: Derek is offering to sell Robert's house
jokes.punchline: 'Shits and gigs' — a malapropism/blend of 'shits and giggles' and 'gigs' — delivered completely naturally as if it's a standard expression
jokes.explanation: A great character-specific malapropism. Derek saying 'shits and gigs' instead of 'shits and giggles' (while seeming to blend it with 'gigs') is perfectly in character for an overconfident bro who has his own mangled idioms. Quotable and well-delivered.

jokes.text: Nancy protests Derek talking about selling the house: 'What about Dale and Brennan? Because they haven't even gotten jobs yet.' / Derek dismisses her: 'God, change the record.'
jokes.setup: Derek is pushing his agenda to sell the house
jokes.punchline: Derek dismisses the concern for his own stepbrother with the contemptuous 'change the record' — confirming he only cares about himself
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat but not particularly inventive — Derek being dismissive is well-established by now.

jokes.text: Robert spots Brennan and Dale sharing a nudie magazine: 'Holy shit, triplets.' — referring to a spread showing three women
jokes.setup: Robert has been talking seriously with Derek about selling the house; he catches a glimpse of the magazine
jokes.punchline: Robert's involuntary, reverential 'Holy shit, triplets' — his seriousness completely punctured by the magazine — is a perfect character moment
jokes.explanation: Robert's involuntary exclamation reveals that he too is not entirely above the man-child behavior. The delivery timing — mid-serious conversation — makes it land perfectly. 'Holy shit, triplets' is very quotable and a great reminder that Robert is human.

jokes.text: Derek arrives at the tree house and greets them: 'What's up, faggots?' — then immediately: 'Whoa, calm down, man. I'm just joking.'
jokes.setup: Derek arrives to greet his brother and stepbrother
jokes.punchline: Derek's casual greeting is an aggressive slur followed by instant deflection — the 'just joking' that characterizes bullies everywhere
jokes.explanation: Character-consistent but the joke is essentially 'Derek is a bully who uses slurs.' The 'just joking' deflection is a recognizable bully pattern. Works for characterization but the comedy is fairly thin.

jokes.text: Derek's CV: 'I made over 550 K last year.' / 'I am the VP of the biggest executive-helicopter-leasing company on the Western Seaboard.' / 'I haven't had a carb since 2004.'
jokes.setup: Dale asks Derek what his problem is
jokes.punchline: Derek's self-introduction is a cascade of status markers that gets progressively weirder — the salary flex, the bizarrely specific job title, and then the no-carb flex as if diet is a professional credential
jokes.explanation: One of the best character-establishment jokes in the film. The structure is perfect: salary (predictable brag) → helicopter-leasing VP (absurdly specific, oddly prestigious) → no carbs since 2004 (completely unexpected, treated as equivalent to the professional achievements). The '2004' specificity is what elevates it — this is a man who tracks his dietary history like a career milestone. Adam Scott delivers this with utter conviction.

jokes.text: Derek presents his abs: 'Check these out. See these boys? This is what I live with. Every day I lather this up with Kiehl's in the shower.'
jokes.setup: Derek has been listing his credentials; now he goes physical
jokes.punchline: Derek lifts his shirt to show his abs, referring to them as 'these boys' — his abs have personhood — and reveals he uses Kiehl's on them, treating them as luxury objects
jokes.explanation: Calling his abs 'these boys' and offering to let people touch them is perfect narcissist comedy. The Kiehl's detail — a recognizable luxury brand — adds the specific pretension that makes it real. The offer to touch ('Sorry, not gonna happen') is a great topper.

jokes.text: Derek admits he 'smoked a J' in the car and is 'feeling a little spacy' — mid-status flex
jokes.setup: Derek has been a relentless status-performer
jokes.punchline: The abrupt confession that he's high slightly undermines everything he's just said, while also being completely in character
jokes.explanation: Good deflation of Derek's persona — he smoked weed before his family visit like a teenager. The 'spacy' confession is funny but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Derek to Dale: 'You wanna punch me right now. You wanna punch me right now, but you won't.' / Then to Brennan: 'You wanna punch me too?'
jokes.setup: Derek has been insufferable all evening; he now reads the room
jokes.punchline: Derek correctly identifies that everyone wants to punch him — and his response is to dare them, which is both insightful and completely deranged
jokes.explanation: Derek's self-awareness about being punchable, combined with his invitation to be punched, is a great character paradox. He knows exactly what he is and leans into it. The escalation to 'Punch me in the fucking face!' being taken literally is a perfect setup for the payoff.

jokes.text: Dale actually punches Derek in the face; Derek falls from the tree house
jokes.setup: Derek has dared everyone to punch him
jokes.punchline: Dale, unlike everyone else his whole life, actually does it — the literal fulfillment of the dare
jokes.explanation: A perfect structural payoff. The setup has been building since Derek arrived — he's been insufferable, the punch dare was literal, and Dale's willingness to actually do it is both satisfying and character-perfect (Dale has no social filter). The fall from the tree house elevates it to full slapstick. The impact is massive because the audience has been wanting this for 10 minutes.

jokes.text: "Oh, shit. / Oh, my shoulder!" — Brennan actually punches Derek and Derek falls from the tree house
jokes.setup: Derek has been demanding to be punched, convinced no one will do it
jokes.punchline: Brennan punches him; Derek falls from the tree house (screaming about his shoulder) — the gag is both the punch landing AND Derek's whimpering response
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured payoff to a long escalating setup. Everything Derek established — his invincibility, his taunting, his abs, his status — collapses in a single punch. 'Oh, my shoulder!' is exactly right: not 'my face' (which would be pride), but 'my shoulder' (injury complaint, vulnerability). The room-reaction impact is very high — this is the payoff the whole Derek sequence has been building to. Well-earned.

jokes.text: Post-punch recovery advice: 'Derek, know what's always good for shoulder pain? If you lick my butthole.'
jokes.setup: Derek is on the ground nursing shoulder pain
jokes.punchline: Brennan offers a fake medical remedy that is actually an insult dressed as concern
jokes.explanation: Good topper on the Derek-getting-punched sequence. The fake-medical framing is a nice absurdist wrapper around a crude insult. 'Snap!' from someone else seals it as a collective triumph.

jokes.text: Derek's exit assessment: 'Aside from that retard trying to punch me, it was a pretty good evening.'
jokes.setup: Dale has successfully punched Derek off a tree house
jokes.punchline: Derek's reframing of being punched in the face as a minor negative in an otherwise 'pretty good evening' is perfect narcissistic denial
jokes.explanation: Derek's resilience — classifying a punch from a tree house as a moderate inconvenience — is excellent character work. His inability to admit being hurt is perfectly consistent with the 'I haven't had a carb since 2004' persona.

jokes.text: Alice approaches Dale privately: 'Is it true you struck Derek in the face and he fell from the tree house?' / 'Yeah. He asked me to.' / 'Oh, that's the most amazing thing I've ever heard.'
jokes.setup: Alice approaches Dale with what seems like a complaint
jokes.punchline: Alice is not angry — she's awed. She finds the punch heroic. The reveal of her perspective completely subverts expectations.
jokes.explanation: A great misdirection — the approach of Derek's wife after the punch reads as confrontational, so the reveal of her being thrilled by it is a satisfying subversion. It also establishes that Derek's own wife hates him, which is the darkest possible joke about the character.

jokes.text: Alice tells Dale: 'I want you to know that tonight I am gonna pleasure myself to the image of you doing that to Derek.' / After Dale looks confused, she clarifies: 'Masturbate. I am.'
jokes.setup: Alice has expressed admiration for Dale punching Derek
