jokes.text: Brennan and Dale are discovered sleepwalking through the Christmas party — parents debate whether to wake them while they cause chaos.
jokes.setup: Robert and Nancy are having a serious marital conversation when the step-sons emerge sleepwalking.
jokes.punchline: The sleepwalking chaos escalates as the parents argue about the myth of waking sleepwalkers while Brennan and Dale apparently destroy the Christmas tree and decorations — the debate itself becoming as farcical as the destruction.
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is primarily visual/physical — inferred from the dialogue reactions ('Oh, the Christmas tree!', 'The pictures! Nancy!'). The structure of the escalating parental debate about sleepwalker mythology while real destruction happens around them is well-constructed farce.

jokes.text: Never, ever wake up a sleepwalker. / That's a myth!
jokes.setup: Brennan and Dale are sleepwalking and causing harm to themselves and the Christmas decorations.
jokes.punchline: The parents get into a heated argument about the sleepwalker mythology (never wake them vs. it's a myth) as a priority ABOVE stopping the actual destruction happening around them.
jokes.explanation: Classic comedy of misplaced priorities — adults arguing about trivia while chaos unfolds. Competently executed but the joke type is familiar.

jokes.text: Robert gets punched/attacked by sleepwalking Dale or Brennan — 'I told you! I told you! Stop it! Don't hurt him! The pictures! Nancy!'
jokes.setup: Robert insists on waking the sleepwalkers against Nancy's warnings.
jokes.punchline: The moment he wakes them, pandemonium — the dialogue ('Stop it! Don't hurt him!') implies Robert gets physically attacked, vindicating Nancy's concern in the most chaotic way.
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy payoff to the sleepwalking escalation. Without seeing the visuals, its impact is diminished in transcript form, but the structure — build to the forbidden action, immediate punishment — is solid classic farce.

jokes.text: We hit this four-point buck. Dead. Lying in the road. Long story short, we sue the state of Michigan. I end up getting 125 G's.
jokes.setup: Derek launches into an anecdote at what appears to be a holiday party gathering.
jokes.punchline: The leap from hitting a deer to successfully suing Michigan for $125,000 is presented as obvious and routine — the legal logic is insane but Derek tells it like it's the most natural conclusion.
jokes.explanation: Derek as an oblivious alpha-bro telling casually insane stories is well-established character comedy. 'Long story short' before an absurd legal outcome is a good structural beat — the phrase promises abbreviation, what follows is still incomprehensible.

jokes.text: You know what I spent that money on? Sniper rifle to hunt deer.
jokes.setup: Derek won $125k suing Michigan over hitting a deer with his car.
jokes.punchline: He spent the settlement money on a sniper rifle — to hunt more deer. The circular, vendetta-fueled logic is delivered with pride.
jokes.explanation: This is the punchline to the deer anecdote and it's genuinely excellent. The structure is a perfect two-beat: setup (ridiculous windfall) → punchline (spent it on a weapon targeting the same species). It's dark, specific, and completely in character for Derek's sociopathic competitiveness. The word 'sniper rifle' rather than 'hunting rifle' adds militaristic escalation that's funnier. High quotability.

jokes.text: Either way, the deers lose, my friends.
jokes.setup: Derek has just explained he sued Michigan over a deer strike and spent the money on a sniper rifle.
jokes.punchline: His philosophical conclusion — 'either way, the deers lose' — delivered to the room as wisdom, the grammatically incorrect 'deers' adding to the oblivious pomposity.
jokes.explanation: The tag to the sniper rifle joke. 'Either way, the deers lose' is a quotable, perfectly economical button. The plural 'deers' (incorrect grammar) suggests Derek's confident ignorance. Delivered as a toast/conclusion ('my friends') adds pompous flair. This and the sniper rifle line together are among the reel's best.

jokes.text: Good riddance. Eat all the damn flowers, anyway.
jokes.setup: Derek has concluded his deer vendetta philosophy.
jokes.punchline: He adds a petty grudge justification — the deer eat flowers — revealing his war on deer has multiple grievances.
jokes.explanation: A good tag that adds another layer to Derek's absurd deer hatred. The specificity of 'eat all the damn flowers' grounds the vendetta in a mundane suburban grievance, which is funnier than a grand reason. Slightly diminished because it's the third beat of the same joke.

jokes.text: If you'll excuse me, I think I'm going to go into the other room to check my hair.
jokes.setup: Derek is holding court at the party; his wife needs to exit.
jokes.punchline: Her excuse — checking her hair in another room — is the thinnest possible pretext, delivered with no apparent awareness of how absurd it sounds.
jokes.explanation: Mild character beat — the wife quietly escaping Derek's monologue is relatable but not particularly crafted. Functions more as a scene breath than a proper joke.

jokes.text: If you'll excuse my space-cadet wife here. Let's just say the meds aren't helping. I'm kidding. Kidding. But not at all.
jokes.setup: Derek's wife excuses herself with a flimsy pretext.
jokes.punchline: Derek publicly jokes that she's on ineffective medication, then immediately backtracks ('kidding') then un-backtracks ('but not at all') — the correction making it worse.
jokes.explanation: The 'I'm kidding. But not at all.' structure is very well done — it perfectly captures the specific sociopathy of someone who uses 'just kidding' as a shield while meaning every word. Derek's character (casual cruelty delivered with confidence) is crystallized here. The rhythm of 'Kidding. Kidding. But not at all.' is itself funny.

jokes.text: Oh, Dale, it's right there. / Shush up, Nancy. I have to get some more bread.
jokes.setup: Dale says he needs to get more gravy; Nancy points out it's right in front of him.
jokes.punchline: Dale tells Nancy to 'shush up' and pivots to needing bread instead — the pivot suggests he knew the gravy was there but needed a reason to move; now 'bread' is the new excuse with equal urgency.
jokes.explanation: Small comedic beat — Dale's 'shush up' is a funny non-word, and the instant pivot from gravy to bread suggests he's just trying to escape a conversation or situation. Mild laugh, functional character work.

jokes.text: What did I do to deserve that? / What do any of us do to deserve anything? I pay enough taxes to support all these lazy goddamn liberals.
jokes.setup: Nancy's rhetorical self-pity question ('What did I do to deserve that?') invites commiseration.
jokes.punchline: Derek answers the rhetorical question philosophically ('What do any of us do to deserve anything?') and then immediately pivots to a non-sequitur rant about taxes and liberals — his version of philosophy.
jokes.explanation: The two-part structure works well: momentary philosophical depth ('What do any of us do to deserve anything?') followed immediately by the most crass possible expansion of that philosophy (tax complaint). It's a perfect Derek beat — he sounds profound for one second.

jokes.text: I couldn't eat another bite of turkey without thinking of you inside of me.
jokes.setup: Alice sneaks away from the party to meet someone (apparently a secret lover) on Christmas.
jokes.punchline: Her romantic/sexual greeting — 'I couldn't eat another bite of turkey without thinking of you inside of me' — is delivered mid-holiday dinner, the juxtaposition of turkey and sex being deliberately crass and funny.
jokes.explanation: The turkey/sex juxtaposition is intentionally crude and works as a shock beat. The specificity of 'another bite of turkey' grounds the horniness in the holiday dinner context amusingly. Fairly cheap but effective.

jokes.text: Come on, let's try something illegal.
jokes.setup: Alice has just made a romantic/sexual overture.
jokes.punchline: The natural follow-up would be something provocative but legal; instead she jumps straight to 'illegal' — reframing the encounter as criminal mischief.
jokes.explanation: Short and punchy. The vagueness of 'something illegal' is funnier than any specific suggestion would be — it implies anything from jaywalking to serious crime. Good economy, mild character specificity.

jokes.text: So, Tommy, what did you get for Christmas? Well, Santa brought me the Bowflex and $1000 in fresh-minted $50 bills. / Wanna know what I got for Christmas? A crushed soul.
jokes.setup: Someone (Tommy) cheerfully reports getting a Bowflex and cash from Santa.
jokes.punchline: Brennan inserts himself with 'Wanna know what I got for Christmas? A crushed soul' — the deflating contrast to Tommy's material happiness.
jokes.explanation: The contrast structure is well-executed: exuberant materialist Christmas haul vs. Brennan's existential devastation. 'A crushed soul' is a great phrase — both melodramatic and oddly precise. The 'Wanna know what I got?' construction invites the listener in before delivering the deflation.

jokes.text: Alice was moving a chair from the living room into the dining room for an extra chair and her back went out. And I just did the best thing, which is get right on the muscles so they don't seize up.
jokes.setup: Dale is found on top of Alice (Derek's wife / his secret lover) with the gathered family watching.
jokes.punchline: Dale offers the most transparent cover story imaginable — she hurt her back moving a chair, he got on top of her to help with the muscles — delivered with absolute earnestness.
jokes.explanation: The more elaborate the excuse, the more obviously guilty he sounds. 'Get right on the muscles' is a funny phrase. The cringe comes from everyone in the room knowing and no one saying it. Competently executed cringe comedy.

jokes.text: It's just a real deep, tight muscle.
jokes.setup: Dale is continuing to sell his cover story about Alice's back injury while he's on top of her.
jokes.punchline: The anatomical description 'real deep, tight muscle' is unintentionally (or entirely intentionally) sexual, causing the cover story to actively incriminate further.
jokes.explanation: Extends the double entendre of the previous beat. Fairly predictable innuendo but the commitment to the bit and Dale's obliviousness makes it work at a functional level.

jokes.text: Hey, sweetie, can you grab me a beer? / I'll get you another Heineken.
jokes.setup: Dale is still on top of Alice in front of the gathered family, in the middle of his cover story.
jokes.punchline: Dale casually asks someone to grab him a beer — mid-scandal, mid-excuse — as if this is a totally normal situation where he'd want refreshment.
jokes.explanation: The request for a beer while caught mid-affair is a perfectly absurd detail. The person's immediate helpful response ('I'll get you another Heineken') adds to the surrealism — everyone is just going along with it.

jokes.text: I got this Mikimoto pearl necklace. But next year I'm gonna ask Santa for breast implants because I'm impatient with my body.
jokes.setup: Asked what she got for Christmas, Tiffany gives an answer appropriate to her character (Derek's materialist world).
jokes.punchline: The pivot from pearl necklace to 'asking Santa for breast implants' because she's 'impatient with her body' — treating cosmetic surgery as a reasonable Christmas list item with the rationale of impatience.
jokes.explanation: The specific phrase 'impatient with my body' is very funny — it frames cosmetic surgery as a logical response to inconvenience rather than vanity. Fits neatly into Derek's social world of casual excess and entitlement.

jokes.text: Hey, Tiffany. Wanna know what I got? A crushed soul. / You mentioned that earlier.
jokes.setup: Brennan tries his 'crushed soul' bit again on a new victim.
jokes.punchline: Tiffany flatly informs him he already said that — the callback becoming a running gag where Brennan's self-pity is more tedious than moving.
jokes.explanation: The callback structure here is elegant: the first 'crushed soul' was a good joke, but making it a running gag that gets called out ('You mentioned that earlier') turns Brennan's melodrama into a commentary on his self-absorption. Tiffany's flat delivery is the punchline. The best kind of callback — it makes the original joke retroactively funnier.

jokes.text: Grant me this one, because I was pretty wasted. So I put my lips around that breathalyzer and I saw those numerals pop up: 0.079.
jokes.setup: Derek is telling another anecdote, apparently about a drunk driving stop.
jokes.punchline: Derek is proud of blowing a 0.079 on a breathalyzer — just under the legal limit — framing it as a victory and achievement rather than a near-miss with criminal charges.
jokes.explanation: The specific number 0.079 (not 0.08) is a funny detail — close enough to be barely legal, specific enough to suggest this has happened before and Derek knows the thresholds. His pride is the joke. Good character-specific humor.

jokes.text: So I started going to Chad Michael Murray's Christmas party.
jokes.setup: Derek's breathalyzer anecdote is interrupted by a non-sequitur about Chad Michael Murray.
jokes.punchline: The name drop of Chad Michael Murray as someone Derek casually attends parties with — a mid-2000s teen heartthrob — is funny in its unexpectedness and in what it says about Derek's social aspirations.
jokes.explanation: Celebrity name-drop jokes are generally cheap, but Chad Michael Murray specifically is a funny choice — not A-list enough to be impressive, specific enough to be absurd. The humor depends heavily on the audience's familiarity with the reference. Moderate.

jokes.text: I could've called this one.
jokes.setup: Brennan and Dale are devastated by the divorce announcement.
jokes.punchline: Derek's immediate smug interjection — 'I could've called this one' — treats family tragedy as a game he's winning.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in-character for Derek — he can't resist the competitive 'I told you so' even at a family meltdown. Brief and efficient. The comedy is entirely in character specificity.

jokes.text: Fuck it, I wanna fucking know! / Let's cut the shit. It is directly your fault.
jokes.setup: Robert and Nancy insist it's not the boys' fault. Brennan demands to know whose fault it really is.
jokes.punchline: Robert immediately abandons the gentle parental script and bluntly says 'It is directly your fault' — the pivot from therapeutic language to blunt assignment of blame is whiplash-funny.
jokes.explanation: The setup is the classic 'it's not your fault' parental script; the inversion — where the parent immediately caves and says yes it absolutely is — is the subversion. The speed of the pivot is what makes it funny. Robert's exasperation overcoming his better instincts is very relatable.

jokes.text: It is absolutely 150 percent your fault! / Of course it's their fault. They're the world's biggest dickheads and they're living in your house.
jokes.setup: Robert has broken and blamed his sons directly for the divorce.
jokes.punchline: Derek gleefully piles on with 'Of course it's their fault. They're the world's biggest dickheads and they're living in your house' — the most antisocial possible support.
jokes.explanation: Derek injecting his opinion into the family breakdown with gleeful cruelty is consistent character comedy. 'World's biggest dickheads' is blunt but the framing (he's supporting Robert while making it worse) is funny.

jokes.text: Mommy! / Dale!
jokes.setup: Brennan and Dale have been told it's their fault their parents are divorcing.
jokes.punchline: Their responses — Brennan crying 'Mommy!' and Dale apparently collapsing — are those of devastated toddlers, not 40-year-old men.
jokes.explanation: The regression to infant behavior — 'Mommy!' — from a 40-year-old man is the film's core joke executed cleanly. Dale apparently physically collapsing ('Dale!') adds physical comedy that's inferred from context. The parallel construction (each boy having a different breakdown mode) is well-staged.

jokes.text: I think I'm going to throw up / Don't throw up / I'm gonna throw it up / You're not gonna throw up / He's gonna throw up / My God, he threw up.
jokes.setup: Brennan announces he might vomit from emotional distress.
jokes.punchline: Despite denials and encouragement not to, he does in fact vomit — the escalating back-and-forth making the inevitability funnier.
jokes.explanation: Classic Chekhov's vomit — if someone says they might throw up enough times in increasingly dramatic terms, they will throw up. The structure of denial/assurance followed by confirmation is well-timed. The 'Oh, this is ugly' reaction is a good button.

jokes.text: All right, dipshits. Right here. One, two, three... / I don't want my picture taken now.
jokes.setup: In the middle of the divorce announcement and Brennan's vomiting breakdown.
jokes.punchline: Derek tries to get a family photo in the middle of the catastrophe; Brennan (who just vomited) protests weakly.
jokes.explanation: Derek attempting to take a family photo immediately after a divorce announcement and a vomiting incident is perfectly in character — his social obliviousness reframed as sociopathy. Brennan's weary 'I don't want my picture taken now' is the right straight-man response. Good character-specific cringe.

jokes.text: You know, we don't have to whisper anymore. Mom and Dad aren't here. / Yeah, but can we keep doing it though? It helps me pretend that they are.
jokes.setup: Brennan and Dale are alone in their room after the parents have left; Brennan notes they don't need to whisper.
jokes.punchline: Dale asks to keep whispering because it helps him pretend the parents are still there — a genuinely sad but funny revelation of his emotional dependence.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes. The request to keep whispering to maintain the illusion of parental presence is both hilarious and genuinely poignant — it encapsulates these characters' arrested development in a single, perfectly economical exchange. The sadness makes the comedy land harder. This is Adam McKay/Will Ferrell at their best: absurd premise with real emotional truth underneath.

jokes.text: If that curly-headed fuck Dale wasn't here, everything would be perfect.
jokes.setup: Brennan recounts what his mother supposedly said about Dale, escalating the blame exchange.
jokes.punchline: Nancy's alleged words — 'that curly-headed fuck Dale' — is a funny, specific insult that doesn't sound like something Nancy would actually say, suggesting Brennan may be embellishing (or Nancy did say it, which is also funny).
jokes.explanation: 'Curly-headed fuck' is a memorably specific insult — the hair detail makes it funnier than a generic expletive. High quotability. The ambiguity about whether Nancy actually said this or Brennan invented it adds an extra layer.

jokes.text: Well, you're a mama's boy who's too chicken to sing in public!
jokes.setup: Brennan has just accused Dale of refusing to take responsibility — the argument is escalating.
jokes.punchline: Dale's counter-accusation — 'too chicken to sing in public' — is a callback to Brennan's secret ambition/shame (his singing voice) and reveals Dale knows exactly what hurts Brennan most.
jokes.explanation: A good callback that weaponizes character detail. The specificity of 'sing in public' as the ultimate insult is funny because it reveals the particular nature of Brennan's shame. It's also absurd that in a fight about parental divorce, the killing blow is about karaoke courage.

jokes.text: Dale broke up Mom and Dad / Dale broke up Mom and Dad / Dale broke up Mom and Dad [sung repeatedly while chasing Dale]
jokes.setup: Brennan retaliates for Dale's insult by turning the blame into a chant/taunt.
jokes.punchline: Brennan chases Dale around while singing/chanting 'Dale broke up Mom and Dad' — a 40-year-old man turning a serious emotional accusation into a playground taunt.
jokes.explanation: The regression to pure childish taunt behavior — turning a real grievance into a singsong chant — is a great embodiment of these characters. The physical chase adds slapstick energy. The repeated chant is itself comedically musical.

jokes.text: It's just like Cold Case Files. It's just like Cold Case Files. It's just like Cold Case Files. People die every day.
jokes.setup: Dale apparently believes Brennan is dead after the fight (Brennan is faking).
jokes.punchline: Dale's immediate frame of reference for dealing with apparent death is a TV crime procedural, which he references three times in a row, then follows with the philosophical shrug 'People die every day.'
jokes.explanation: Saying 'Cold Case Files' three times in a row is funny rhythmically — it's the comedic repetition rule. Then the pivot to 'People die every day' as a coping shrug is a beautiful character moment. Dale's emotional processing (TV reference → grim acceptance → planning to bury him) reveals his stunted worldview perfectly. High originality for the specific Cold Case Files choice.

jokes.text: Brennan! You're alive! Oh, my God. / I know. I'm alive.
jokes.setup: Dale has been grieving Brennan and planning his burial.
jokes.punchline: Brennan reveals he was faking — Dale's disproportionate shock ('You're alive! Oh, my God!') and Brennan's casual 'I know. I'm alive.' creates a perfect comic exchange.
jokes.explanation: Brennan's flat 'I know. I'm alive.' is the perfect response to Dale's hysteria. The economy of that response — the casual confirmation of his own aliveness — is very funny. Great rhythm between the two performers.

jokes.text: I was faking. I used ninja focus to slow my heart rate down.
jokes.setup: Dale is shocked Brennan was faking death; Brennan explains how.
jokes.punchline: 'Ninja focus' as the technique used to fake death — Brennan presents this with complete sincerity, as if ninja heart-rate control is a recognized method.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and originality. 'Ninja focus' is a brilliantly absurd concept delivered with absolute conviction. It implies Brennan has been practicing this, has a name for it, and considers it a legitimate skill. The specificity of 'slow my heart rate down' as the goal adds technical-sounding absurdity. Very high quotability — this line is memorable and repeatable.

jokes.text: What are you doing? / I'm burying you. / I'm alive. Brennan, I'm alive. / You're waking the neighbors!
jokes.setup: Brennan has just revealed he's alive; Dale is apparently still going ahead with the burial.
jokes.punchline: Dale continues trying to bury the living Brennan; when Brennan objects, Dale's priority concern is waking the neighbors — not the fact that he's burying an alive person.
jokes.explanation: Dale continuing the burial after the reveal is a great absurdist escalation — his plan has momentum and he's committed to it. The 'You're waking the neighbors' rebuke is the perfect wrong priority — Dale's concern is social propriety about noise, not about literally burying his living stepbrother. Excellent structure.

jokes.text: Close your eyes. Let the dirt just shower over you. / This is your fault. / Oh, I'm exhausted. I'm gonna sleep good tonight.
jokes.setup: Dale is literally burying the living Brennan.
jokes.punchline: Dale's soothing instructions ('Let the dirt just shower over you') followed by his post-burial exhaustion ('I'm gonna sleep good tonight') — treating burying a live person as a satisfying evening's physical labor.
jokes.explanation: 'Let the dirt just shower over you' as a soothing instruction is hilariously inappropriate tenderness toward someone being buried alive. The pivot to 'I'm gonna sleep good tonight' — the satisfaction of a task completed — is a perfect, deadpan button to the whole sequence.

jokes.text: Don't you touch my drums! / Zombie! Zombie! Zombie!
jokes.setup: Brennan has emerged from his burial (or begun escaping) and apparently moved toward Dale's drums.
jokes.punchline: Dale's immediate terror — screaming 'Zombie! Zombie! Zombie!' — treats the emerging-from-dirt Brennan as an actual undead threat, despite having just buried him seconds ago.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from burial completion to zombie panic is a great comedic gear-shift. Dale has no cognitive dissonance about the fact that he just buried this person — when Brennan emerges, Dale's frame immediately shifts to supernatural horror. The drums concern ('Don't you touch my drums!') is also a perfect character-specific priority.

jokes.text: I'm late for school.
jokes.setup: Dale and Brennan are wrestling/fighting after the zombie scare, apparently in a full grapple.
jokes.punchline: Dale, mid-fight, announces 'I'm late for school' — a completely non-sequitur statement that (a) he's 40 and doesn't go to school, and (b) is offered as a reason to disengage, mid-physical-altercation.
jokes.explanation: Four words, enormous character comedy. A 40-year-old man saying 'I'm late for school' mid-fight is a perfect encapsulation of his infantilized worldview — he literally lives in a child's mental framework. The economy is exceptional. High quotability.

jokes.text: I will kiss you right on the mouth, Kenny Rogers.
jokes.setup: Dale is still entangled with Brennan after the fight/wrestling.
jokes.punchline: Dale, apparently in a moment of exasperated affection, threatens/promises to kiss Brennan 'right on the mouth' and calls him Kenny Rogers — a non-sequitur celebrity comparison with no apparent logic.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's most quotable lines. 'I will kiss you right on the mouth, Kenny Rogers' works because (a) the mouth-kiss threat is itself absurd, (b) 'Kenny Rogers' as a nickname for Brennan comes from nowhere but somehow fits his slightly disheveled, bearded quality, and (c) the combination of affection and randomness is very Dale. The specificity of 'right on the mouth' vs. a cheek is funnier.

jokes.text: Hey. We're no longer brothers. We never were. We were stepbrothers.
jokes.setup: Brennan is breaking off his relationship with Dale after their fight and the parental divorce.
jokes.punchline: Brennan's dramatic 'We're no longer brothers' is immediately undercut by his own technical correction — 'We never were. We were stepbrothers' — deflating the drama with a legal/semantic clarification.
jokes.explanation: Structurally very clean: dramatic declaration → self-correction that punctures the drama. The comedy is in Brennan undercutting his own big moment by being technically accurate. The title of the film being invoked at this moment adds ironic self-reference. Very quotable. Among the reel's best lines.

jokes.text: That was one of your best. / These balls fucking suck.
jokes.setup: Some kind of sports/activity is happening; someone compliments Derek on a shot.
jokes.punchline: Derek's immediate complaint — 'These balls fucking suck' — ignores the compliment entirely, focused on equipment grievances.
jokes.explanation: Minor character beat. Derek refusing to accept a compliment and complaining about equipment is in-character but not a strongly constructed joke. Transition moment more than a real joke.

jokes.text: TJ, get an office pool going. Give Ken-Doll Crotch here two weeks, tops.
jokes.setup: Brennan shows up at Derek's workplace asking for a job.
jokes.punchline: Derek's immediate response is to start an office betting pool on when Brennan will fail — and his nickname for Brennan is 'Ken-Doll Crotch,' suggesting Brennan has some kind of anatomical smoothness or generic blandness.
jokes.explanation: 'Ken-Doll Crotch' is a memorably specific insult. The office pool for predicting Brennan's failure before he's even hired is a great Derek power move. The name combines Derek's cruelty with an oddly anatomical imagination.

jokes.text: Do I carry my high-school diploma around? What do you do with your hair? What happens if there's inclement weather? Where do you...? What do you wear? Can you wash clothes in the dishwasher?
jokes.setup: Brennan is asking his therapist/Dr. Angel Face for help becoming a grown-up.
jokes.punchline: His list of questions about adult life reveals he literally does not know how to function as an adult — the dishwasher clothes question being the peak of the escalation.
jokes.explanation: The escalating list of adult-life questions is well-constructed comedy — each question is more fundamental and revealing than the last, culminating in 'Can you wash clothes in the dishwasher?' which is the perfect absurd peak. The structure builds well and each beat earns its laugh.

jokes.text: I notice there's a long gap in your job history and it said for 22 years you went Kerouac on everyone's ass.
jokes.setup: Dr. Angel Face is reviewing Brennan's résumé for a job.
jokes.punchline: The résumé apparently describes 22 years of unemployment as 'went Kerouac on everyone's ass' — Brennan (or someone) wrote a literary/beatnik justification for two decades of doing nothing.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. 'Went Kerouac on everyone's ass' as a résumé description of unemployment is both a great phrase (literary reference deployed absurdly in a corporate context) and a perfect character reveal. It suggests either Brennan wrote this himself (delusional self-presentation) or someone helped him dress up his inertia in Beat Generation terms. Very quotable. 'On everyone's ass' appended to a Kerouac reference is a funny collision of registers.

jokes.text: I'm gonna be honest with you. I really need a job. And I will take any position, as long as it doesn't involve having sex with old ladies for money or bear traps. Those are my two bugaboos.
jokes.setup: Brennan is desperate for a job and states his terms.
jokes.punchline: His two dealbreakers — 'having sex with old ladies for money' and 'bear traps' — are presented as equivalent and reasonable workplace concerns, with 'bugaboos' as the bizarrely genteel word to describe them.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes and among the film's most quotable lines. The pairing of 'having sex with old ladies for money' (vaguely understandable concern) with 'bear traps' (completely insane, non-occupational hazard) as equivalent dealbreakers is brilliantly absurd. The word 'bugaboos' — formal, slightly Victorian, used to describe these two specific concerns — is the perfect button. The joke is specific, character-consistent (Brennan's earnest absurdism), and has tremendous originality.

jokes.text: I will take any position, as long as it doesn't involve having sex with old ladies for money or bear traps. Those are my two bugaboos.
jokes.setup: Brennan is telling an employment agent how flexible he is about job types.
jokes.punchline: His exclusions are 'sex with old ladies for money' and 'bear traps' — a baffling and unequal list of dealbreakers that he calmly labels 'my two bugaboos.'
jokes.explanation: One of the film's funniest moments in this reel. The genius is in the pairing: 'sex with old ladies for money' is at least a recognizable thing to be excluded from, but 'bear traps' is completely left-field — why would a temp job involve bear traps? The word 'bugaboos' applied to these two specific concerns is perfect character voice. The juxtaposition of a known bad thing with a bizarre non-sequitur bad thing is impeccable comedy construction. Near the top of this reel's scoring.

jokes.text: There's a catering business, there's a temp job open. And you get to play with fire.
jokes.setup: Dr. Angel Face responds to Brennan's unusual job requirements by listing openings.
jokes.punchline: She adds 'And you get to play with fire' as a selling point for one of the jobs — suggesting she's already adapted her pitch to what will motivate Brennan specifically.
jokes.explanation: The therapist/job counselor's understanding that 'playing with fire' is a valid incentive for Brennan is both funny and reveals she knows exactly what kind of person she's dealing with. Good economy.

jokes.text: What do you want? This is my online-poker time.
jokes.setup: Brennan approaches Derek at work about the Catalina Wine Mixer.
jokes.punchline: Derek's work hours are apparently reserved for online poker — his professional priorities are as inverted as everyone else's in this world.
jokes.explanation: Minor character beat — Derek treating online poker as sacred work time is consistent with his character as a fraud. Good economy but not a heavily constructed joke.

jokes.text: I've been earning and burning, snapping necks and cashing checks.
jokes.setup: Brennan is pitching himself as ready for the Catalina Wine Mixer challenge.
jokes.punchline: His self-aggrandizing phrase 'earning and burning, snapping necks and cashing checks' applies tough-guy business slang to someone who has done nothing — the language of a successful hustler from a career shut-in.
jokes.explanation: 'Snapping necks and cashing checks' has become one of the film's most quoted lines. The rhythm and rhyme scheme (earning/burning, snapping/cashing) gives it a cadence that makes it instantly memorable. The irony of Brennan saying this is perfect character comedy — he's never earned or burned anything. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Screw it, let's let him do it. It's a win-win for me... because if you fuck up, Brennan, I get to fire your ass. But if you pull it off, I look like a genius to the board.
jokes.setup: Derek deliberates whether to give Brennan the Catalina Wine Mixer job.
jokes.punchline: His reasoning is entirely self-serving — he articulates his win-win openly to Brennan's face, with no pretense of benevolence.
jokes.explanation: Derek's naked self-interest stated openly is consistent character comedy. The honesty of his cynicism is funnier than if he pretended to be doing Brennan a favor. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: It's the Catalina fucking Wine Mixer, okay?
jokes.setup: Derek is briefing Brennan on the importance of the event.
jokes.punchline: The Catalina Wine Mixer is treated with awe and reverence, the profanity ('fucking') inserted mid-name as an intensifier, suggesting this is how Derek always says it.
jokes.explanation: The Catalina Wine Mixer becomes a running joke through how reverently it's spoken of. The embedded profanity ('the Catalina fucking Wine Mixer') as a fixed phrase — not an adjective but baked into the name — is a funny verbal tic. This phrase will recur and each repetition adds to the gag.

jokes.text: Are you saying 'pow'? What are you saying?
jokes.setup: Brennan apparently punctuates one of his statements with 'pow' as an exclamation.
jokes.punchline: Derek's irritated genuine confusion about the 'pow' — he doesn't know if it's intentional or what it means — is funnier than any explanation of the 'pow' could be.
jokes.explanation: The meta-confusion about Brennan's verbal tic is a good reaction-beat joke. The audience doesn't know what 'pow' was either, which makes Derek's confusion a shared experience. Efficient.

jokes.text: Are you saying 'pow'? What are you saying?
jokes.setup: Brennan apparently makes some kind of exclamatory sound or gesture of agreement.
jokes.punchline: Derek is baffled by whatever Brennan is doing — the question 'Are you saying "pow"?' suggests Brennan's enthusiasm has taken a sound-effect form.
jokes.explanation: Minor reaction beat — Derek's bafflement at Brennan's enthusiasm-noise is a decent beat. The specificity of 'pow' as the guessed sound is funny.

jokes.text: It's the biggest helicopter-leasing event in the Western Hemisphere since 1997.
jokes.setup: Derek is explaining the magnitude of the Catalina Wine Mixer.
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'since 1997' and the grandeur of 'Western Hemisphere' applied to helicopter leasing creates a perfectly absurd scale of importance for a niche corporate event.
jokes.explanation: The 'since 1997' specification is the key joke — implying there was a bigger helicopter-leasing event in the Western Hemisphere at some point but 1997 was a particularly good year. The absurd specificity of this niche record is well-executed.

jokes.text: I have to sell or lease at least 80 choppers to make my nut. And you mess with my nut, Brennan, Randy here is gonna eat your dick. Like Kobayashi. I've seen him do it.
jokes.setup: Derek explains the stakes of the Catalina Wine Mixer to Brennan.
jokes.punchline: The threat escalates from business stakes ('make my nut') to 'Randy here is gonna eat your dick. Like Kobayashi' — referencing the competitive eater as the standard of speed/thoroughness — and 'I've seen him do it' as a witness confirmation.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes. The Kobayashi reference (competitive hot dog eater) applied to penis-eating as a threat is brilliantly absurd and specific. 'Like Kobayashi' is a perfect simile that creates a vivid, insane image. 'I've seen him do it' as Randy's credential is an extraordinary tag — it confirms the threat with eyewitness testimony delivered straight. The escalation from business stakes to this specific threat is very well structured.

jokes.text: You've seen him eat a penis? / It was in international waters, so they couldn't prosecute him.
jokes.setup: Brennan questions Derek's claim that he witnessed Randy eat a penis.
jokes.punchline: Derek explains the legal jurisdiction context — it was in international waters, so there was no prosecution — treating this as the relevant detail, not the act itself.
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the reel. The 'international waters' explanation is a perfect response — it treats the act of penis-eating as a legal/jurisdictional matter rather than something worth explaining on its own terms. The implication that Randy has eaten penises in international waters specifically to avoid prosecution reveals an entire backstory that is insane and funny on multiple levels. Derek's casual confirmation ('so they couldn't prosecute him') as if this is the relevant clarification is the kind of absurdist escalation that becomes legendary. Approaches the gold standard anchor quality.

jokes.text: Because I wanna make bank, bro. I wanna get ass. And I wanna drive a Range Rover.
jokes.setup: Derek asks Brennan why he wants the Catalina Wine Mixer job so badly.
jokes.punchline: Brennan's honest answer — make money, get sex, drive a Range Rover — is delivered with the earnest, unironic sincerity of someone who genuinely thinks these are profound motivations.
jokes.explanation: The three-part list structure works — 'make bank, get ass, drive a Range Rover' has good rhythmic escalation. The Range Rover as the peak aspiration (not more money or more success, specifically a Range Rover) is a funny specific detail. 'I wanna get ass, bro' from a 40-year-old man-child is good character work.

jokes.text: I don't know what it is, but I wanna deliver one of these right in your suck hole.
jokes.setup: Randy is complimenting Brennan on running the Catalina Wine Mixer well.
jokes.punchline: His affection is expressed as a threat/desire to punch Brennan in the face — 'your suck hole' — delivered while simultaneously praising him, the violence being his love language.
jokes.explanation: 'Suck hole' is an inspired coinage for 'mouth' — specific, grotesque, and funnier than 'face.' The structure (praise → violent expression of affection) is a good joke shape. Randy as a character who expresses positive emotions through threats is a consistent comedic choice.

jokes.text: Is there anything I can do? / No. Not really. It's your face. / Again, you're doing great, man. The Catalina Wine Mixer. / But if you don't change your face, I'm gonna change it for you.
jokes.setup: Randy is giving Brennan contradictory feedback at the event.
jokes.punchline: Randy simultaneously praises Brennan's work and threatens to physically alter his face — the incoherence of 'you're doing great / change your face or I'll change it' as feedback is very funny.
jokes.explanation: The running bit about Randy's objection to Brennan's face — a thing Brennan cannot change — escalates well. 'If you don't change your face, I'm gonna change it for you' is a good threat structure. The juxtaposition of the compliment and the face threat is the joke.

jokes.text: All I can do is take that in, consider it, and I'll just do my best version of whatever I think that would be.
jokes.setup: Randy has just told Brennan his face is the problem and implied he wants to punch it.
jokes.punchline: Brennan responds with sincere corporate-speak — 'take that in, consider it, do my best version' — applying professional language to an impossible personal feedback.
jokes.explanation: Brennan applying professional development language to the feedback 'your face is punchable' is a great character moment — he's trying so hard to be a functioning adult that he processes everything through HR-speak. 'My best version of whatever I think that would be' applied to changing your face is absurdist and character-specific.

jokes.text: I don't even hear you, your face is driving me nuts.
jokes.setup: Brennan is explaining how he'll try to work on his face.
jokes.punchline: Randy cannot even process what Brennan is saying because Brennan's face is too distracting/offensive to him.
jokes.explanation: Third beat of the face running gag. Each iteration escalates Randy's face-fixation — from comment to threat to inability to hear words. The escalation structure works; this is the softest of the three beats but lands because the gag has built.

jokes.text: I don't even hear you, your face is driving me nuts.
jokes.setup: Brennan has just responded thoughtfully to the face-criticism.
jokes.punchline: Randy reveals he literally couldn't hear what Brennan said because the face was too distracting.
jokes.explanation: A good tag to the face sequence — Randy's distraction has escalated to blocking out all other sensory input. 'I don't even hear you' is funny because Brennan just said something earnest and thoughtful. The escalation from 'want to punch' to 'can't hear you' is good comedic progression.

jokes.text: We are Uptown Girl. We are California's preeminent 1980s Billy Joel cover band.
jokes.setup: A band introduces themselves at the Catalina Wine Mixer.
jokes.punchline: The band is named 'Uptown Girl' — not 'Piano Man' or 'Billy Joel Experience' but specifically the one song title that is NOT their own (it's Billy Joel but not Piano Man, their most famous song) — and they describe themselves as 'California's preeminent' Billy Joel cover band, implying a competitive field.
jokes.explanation: 'Preeminent' as self-description for a cover band is funny — it suggests there's a ranking system for Billy Joel tribute acts in California. The name 'Uptown Girl' rather than something more obviously Joel-branded is a specific absurd choice.

jokes.text: I hope you are, because sometimes life can be tough. And I know that sometimes it's hard to 'Keeping the Faith.'
jokes.setup: The Uptown Girl frontman addresses the crowd and asks if they're having a good time.
jokes.punchline: He delivers a motivational platitude — 'sometimes it's hard' — and pivots it into a song title plug ('Keeping the Faith,' a Billy Joel '80s song), the seamless splice of life advice and self-promotion.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from sincere life observation to song-title plug is well-executed. The fact that it's their closing line (the reel ends here) gives it a nice button energy. 'Keeping the Faith' works both as a cliché and as a song title, which is a clean double meaning.

jokes.text: Robert asks if Brennan still has his night-vision goggles; Brennan says he had to sell them to pay for car insurance.
jokes.setup: Robert and Brennan are catching up like old friends, and Robert asks a nostalgic question about night-vision goggles — an absurdly specific item to associate with friendship memories.
jokes.punchline: Brennan had to sell them to pay for car insurance — framing the goggles as a totally normal possession and the sale as a mundane adult financial decision.
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of night-vision goggles as a casual friendship artifact is funny, and the punchline grounds it in a mundane adult reality (car insurance), which makes both details funnier by collision. Character-specific in that it treats this bizarre equipment as normal without comment.

jokes.text: Robert asks if Brennan is still kicking holes in pumpkins; Brennan says no, but he started taking baby aspirin for his heart.
jokes.setup: Robert catalogues the childlike/violent activities they used to share — board-breaking, pumpkin-kicking — implying Brennan will confirm or deny continued adolescent behavior.
jokes.punchline: Brennan pivots to a hyper-adult health concern: baby aspirin for heart attack prevention. The juxtaposition of infantile destruction and geriatric preventive care in a ~40-year-old is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'kicking holes in pumpkins' to 'baby aspirin for my heart' is a genuinely well-structured misdirect. The setup dangles expected manchild behavior and the punchline delivers unexpected middle-aged hypochondria — both are absurd for the same person, and the combination crystallizes the film's core joke about men stuck between boyhood and decrepitude.

jokes.text: Robert tells his golf buddy 'It's a truly funny observation' — delivered flatly as the two men have apparently been discussing something mundane.
jokes.setup: We cut into what appears to be a dry, polite adult-party conversation between Robert and an unnamed man.
jokes.punchline: Robert's sincere, stiff declaration that something is 'a truly funny observation' is funnier than whatever the observation was — the formality and over-earnestness of the compliment undercuts the content entirely.
jokes.explanation: A mild character-comedy beat — Robert's stilted social politeness is a recurring gag. Gets a mild laugh but doesn't add much.

jokes.text: Robert suggests they 'grab a bite to eat' at Outback Steakhouse, adding 'I've grown very fond of that place.'
jokes.setup: Robert and Nancy have just had a warm, emotionally resonant reunion with their sons at the Catalina Wine Mixer.
jokes.punchline: Robert's sincere declaration of fondness for Outback Steakhouse as the logical culmination of their emotional reunion is aggressively banal — the gap between emotional stakes and chain restaurant enthusiasm is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Robert's oblivious earnestness about Outback Steakhouse is a reliable character beat — he's the kind of man for whom a chain restaurant represents a genuine treat. The specificity of 'grown very fond of' elevates it slightly above generic.

jokes.text: Robert says 'I think Brennan organized this whole thing to get us back together' — then immediately: 'You have to excuse me. I think that I just might cry.'
jokes.setup: Robert has just made a heartwarming observation about Brennan's motivations.
jokes.punchline: He announces his imminent crying with the same matter-of-fact tone he uses for everything — no emotional build, just a clinical announcement followed by 'It's the funniest thing. Bye-bye.'
jokes.explanation: 'It's the funniest thing. Bye-bye.' is a perfectly odd exit line — Richard Jenkins playing Robert's emotional leakage with absolute deadpan dignity is a consistent source of gentle comedy. The abrupt 'Bye-bye' is the best word in the sequence.

jokes.text: A party guest shouts 'Start the Fire, buddy!' at the '80s Billy Joel cover band; someone else demands 'Play something from The Stranger!'
jokes.setup: An '80s Billy Joel cover band is performing at an upscale corporate mixer.
jokes.punchline: The guests argue over which era of Billy Joel they want — 'We Didn't Start the Fire' (1989) vs. 'The Stranger' (1977) — establishing the band's pedantic '80s-only rule before the confrontation.
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the bigger confrontation that follows. Mildly amusing in isolation because of the specificity of Billy Joel era-pedantry.

jokes.text: The band singer screams 'Hey, listen, motherfucker, we only sing '80s Joel! So take your skank hooker wife and get the fuck out of here!'
jokes.setup: The party guest has pushed back on the band's '80s-only rule; a polite disagreement at a corporate event seems likely.
jokes.punchline: The singer absolutely detonates — full profanity, the 'skank hooker wife' insult — at a formal wine mixer. The gap between the high-class setting and this volcanic response is enormous.
jokes.explanation: The sheer disproportionality of the response — a cover band singer going nuclear over Billy Joel era-specificity at a wine mixer — is very funny. The specificity of 'skank hooker wife' (unprovoked, escalatory) earns the extra impact. Pure escalation comedy.

jokes.text: Derek to Brennan: 'Hey, great job, fuck face. You just busted my nut. This party's shot.'
jokes.setup: The band has just been ejected/stormed off; Derek is furious at Brennan for presumably booking them.
jokes.punchline: 'You just busted my nut' — a crude idiom deployed with corporate fury by the aggressively alpha Derek, who then uses 'Audi 5000' as a dismissal, an absurd period-piece slang choice.
jokes.explanation: Derek's dialect of business-bro aggression ('busted my nut,' 'Audi 5000') is a consistent character joke. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Derek fires Brennan and says 'You're Audi 5000, my friend' as a dismissal.
jokes.setup: Derek is enraged and firing Brennan on the spot at the Catalina Wine Mixer.
jokes.punchline: 'You're Audi 5000, my friend' — a dated, mid-80s slang term for 'you're out of here,' delivered with icy corporate finality. The absurdity of using that phrase in this context, plus the incongruous 'my friend,' lands.
jokes.explanation: Adam Scott's delivery of period-inappropriate slang with dead seriousness is part of Derek's comedic DNA. Mild laugh, mostly character work.

jokes.text: Brennan, devastated: 'Robert, you don't get it. It's the Catalina Wine Mixer! People have killed to be in the position I'm in.'
jokes.setup: Robert tries to minimize Brennan being fired, suggesting it's no big deal.
jokes.punchline: Brennan's hysterical insistence on the mythic importance of the Catalina Wine Mixer — 'people have KILLED to be in the position I'm in' — is a perfect character moment of deranged self-importance about a helicopter sales event.
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most quotable lines. 'People have KILLED to be in the position I'm in' is a perfect Brennan line — genuine delusion, complete sincerity, and the gap between the grandiosity of the claim and the reality (a corporate helicopter mixer) is enormous. High quotability, strong character integration.

jokes.text: Robert's speech about wanting to be a Tyrannosaurus Rex as a child — 'I made my arms short and I roamed the backyard and I chased the neighborhood cats and I growled and I roared.'
jokes.setup: Robert is trying to give an inspiring speech about not giving up on your dreams to motivate Dale and Brennan to perform.
jokes.punchline: His dream is not music or art or adventure — it's being a T. Rex. And he acted on it physically: short arms, prowling, chasing cats. The specificity and commitment of the childhood fantasy is the joke.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional. Richard Jenkins delivering a sincere, heartfelt aspirational speech about wanting to be a T. Rex — with genuine emotional stakes attached — is a perfect collision of the absurd and the earnest. The details (short arms, chasing cats) are specific enough to feel improvised and lived-in. 'Don't lose your dinosaur' becomes an accidental profundity. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its specificity and unexpectedness; the character integration pushes it slightly above.

jokes.text: Robert clarifies: 'He didn't really say that. He said, Stop being a dinosaur and get a job.'
jokes.setup: Robert has just delivered the touching line 'Bobby, you're 17. It's time to throw childish things aside' — a poignant paraphrase of his father's advice.
jokes.punchline: He immediately corrects himself: his dad actually said 'Stop being a dinosaur and get a job.' The literal version is both harsher and funnier — it confirms that the T. Rex thing was real enough that his father had to specifically address it.
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural beat: the first version is a touching paraphrase, the immediate correction reveals the blunt, specific, undeniable reality. 'Stop being a dinosaur and get a job' is funnier than anything Robert could have invented because it's plausible as actual father-to-son speech. The economy (one sentence demolishes the sentiment) and the callback to the T. Rex premise make this among the reel's best constructed jokes.

jokes.text: 'Don't lose your dinosaur.'
jokes.setup: Robert has just told the story of his childhood T. Rex fantasy and his father telling him to give it up.
jokes.punchline: His motivational summary — the takeaway message — is 'Don't lose your dinosaur.' Delivered with complete sincerity as life wisdom.
jokes.explanation: Four words that land as both genuinely moving and completely ridiculous. This is the film's thesis statement delivered in the most absurd possible frame. 'Don't lose your dinosaur' is the kind of line that gets put on shirts. Perfect economy — could not be shorter. Character integration is as high as it gets: only Robert Doback, who literally wanted to be a T. Rex, could deliver this with enough sincerity to make it funny AND touching. This is a legitimate 8+ moment by the calibration standard.

jokes.text: Robert confirms: 'You could never be a dinosaur. Yeah.' — agreeing that T. Rex is not achievable, as the final word on the matter.
jokes.setup: Dale has just asked how being a T. Rex could be a skill one could come back to.
jokes.punchline: Robert concedes the literal point immediately — 'You could never be a dinosaur' — as if that was always understood and doesn't undercut his speech at all.
jokes.explanation: The concession lands because Robert treats it as an entirely unimportant caveat to his inspiring speech. The absurdist premise is acknowledged as reality without destabilizing his sincerity.

jokes.text: Brennan: 'I'm so scared right now. I'm gonna do what's sensible: I'm gonna file for unemployment and try to get a job at Enterprise Rent-A-Car. Because they got an excellent corporate structure and they give you the tools to be your own boss.'
jokes.setup: Robert has just delivered an inspiring speech; everyone expects Brennan to rise to the occasion.
jokes.punchline: Brennan retreats into an earnest, detailed pitch for Enterprise Rent-A-Car as a career path — his version of 'sensible' is a corporate car rental franchise, delivered with genuine enthusiasm for 'the tools to be your own boss.'
jokes.explanation: Classic Brennan: his version of a safety net is a mid-tier car rental company. The specific detail of 'excellent corporate structure' and 'tools to be your own boss' — HR brochure language delivered as genuine aspiration — is both funny and deeply sad. Strong character integration: this could only be Brennan.

jokes.text: Brennan's reversal: 'My dad's right. This isn't me. I'm fucking miserable. I had to get up at 10:00 this morning.'
jokes.setup: Brennan has just argued for the sensible Enterprise Rent-A-Car path; now he pivots to inspiration.
jokes.punchline: His evidence for being 'fucking miserable' — the proof that he is not living his authentic life — is that he had to get up at 10:00 AM. His threshold for suffering is a 10 AM wake-up.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in this reel. 'I'm fucking miserable — I had to get up at 10:00 this morning' is a perfectly compressed character statement: Brennan's entire crisis is that adulthood requires waking up at 10 AM. The gap between the magnitude of his complaint ('fucking miserable') and the cause (a 10 AM alarm) is enormous and perfectly calibrated. High quotability, exceptional character integration.

jokes.text: Robert, watching Dale walk toward the stage: 'This crowd's gonna eat him alive.'
jokes.setup: Robert has just inspired Dale with the 'don't lose your dinosaur' speech; Dale is heading to the stage.
jokes.punchline: Robert's immediate assessment — delivered as a matter-of-fact observation, not a warning — undercuts the inspirational moment with blunt realism.
jokes.explanation: Robert's deadpan doom-saying immediately after his own inspiring speech is a nice bit of self-contradiction. His total lack of confidence in what he just engineered is characteristically Richard Jenkins.

jokes.text: Dale takes the stage at the Catalina Wine Mixer and announces: 'My name's Dale Doback, and I hope you like to kick it.'
jokes.setup: Dale has just walked onto the stage of a formal corporate helicopter sales event as an uninvited performer.
jokes.punchline: 'I hope you like to kick it' — delivered with complete earnestness by a 40-year-old man about to perform at an event where he has no business being — is both endearing and catastrophically tone-deaf.
jokes.explanation: The formal introduction of himself by full name ('Dale Doback') at a corporate event he's crashing, followed by 'I hope you like to kick it,' is a perfectly calibrated cringe setup. The audience's instant revulsion ('Get off the stage, you dick!') validates the joke.

jokes.text: Dale begins performing 'Boats and Hoes' — an original song from his 'Prestige Worldwide' music video — solo at the Catalina Wine Mixer to immediate crowd hostility.
jokes.setup: 'Boats and Hoes' was established as Dale and Brennan's absurd vanity music video project from earlier in the film.
jokes.punchline: Dale performing this song — written for a home video — at a formal corporate event as a sincere artistic statement is the full cringe payoff of everything that has been building.
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff of 'Boats and Hoes' in this context — Dale alone on a stage being screamed at to get off, still going — is a strong earned comedy moment. The song's absurdity combined with Dale's sincerity and the crowd's hostility creates a classic cringe climax.

jokes.text: Crowd immediately heckles: 'Get off the stage, you dick!' — followed by 'Terrible! Terrible!'
jokes.setup: Dale has just launched into his rap with sincere enthusiasm.
jokes.punchline: The crowd's instant, unanimous, specific rejection — not just booing but 'Terrible! Terrible!' — is the comedic counterweight to Dale's earnestness.
jokes.explanation: The crowd reaction provides necessary comic contrast. 'Terrible! Terrible!' repeated is funnier than a single 'terrible.' Functional escalation.

jokes.text: Crowd chants: 'Dale has a mangina! Dale has a mangina!'
jokes.setup: Dale is being heckled on stage at the Catalina Wine Mixer.
jokes.punchline: The crowd somehow knows about the 'mangina' — a callback to the earlier scene where Dale tucked himself and traumatized Brennan. The fact that this private incident is now a crowd chant is surreal.
jokes.explanation: Strong callback — the fact that this crowd knows about Dale's mangina is never explained and doesn't need to be. The absurdity of the chant at a wine mixer adds to the surreal escalation.

jokes.text: Nancy's reaction to Dale being chanted at: 'He's up there alone, Brennan. He's up there alone.'
jokes.setup: Dale is being brutalized by the crowd. Nancy watches helplessly.
jokes.punchline: Nancy's emotional appeal — 'he's up there alone' — treats Dale's self-inflicted public humiliation as a tragedy requiring rescue, with the same maternal urgency as a child lost in a crowd.
jokes.explanation: Mary Steenburgen's maternal panic over a 40-year-old man's self-caused onstage disaster is a reliable joke in this film. 'He's up there alone' said twice with increasing urgency is an effective comedic pressure valve.

jokes.text: Brennan jumps on stage despite being told not to — Nancy: 'What did you do?' Robert: 'Oh, Jesus, Nancy. I couldn't stand to see him like that. I miss my son.'
jokes.setup: Brennan has just crashed the stage to rescue Dale; Nancy is horrified.
jokes.punchline: Robert immediately reverses — 'I miss my son' — as if his entire inspiring speech and Dale's public humiliation are just the inconvenient backstory to his desire to be near Brennan. Pure emotional incontinence.
jokes.explanation: Robert's instant pivoting between pride and sentimentality is consistent character comedy. 'I miss my son' is a good button.

jokes.text: Dale, before Brennan joins: 'Let me go for a few bars. Come in soft, but then finish strong.' / 'Thanks for coming up.' / 'You got it, Dragon.'
jokes.setup: Dale is being savaged on stage and Brennan is rushing up to help; a quick emotional rescue might be expected.
jokes.punchline: Dale treats this as a professional musical handoff, giving Brennan technical stage direction ('come in soft, but then finish strong') and using the affectionate nickname 'Dragon.' The competence of the direction vs. the chaos of the situation is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Dale's calm professional pivot mid-public-humiliation — giving technical stage direction while being booed — is a beautiful character moment. 'You got it, Dragon' as the nickname lands warmly and absurdly. This is the film's bromance in miniature.

jokes.text: The extended 'Boats and Hoes' performance transforms the hostile crowd into a cheering, dancing audience — a full-crowd musical reversal.
jokes.setup: Dale has been booed off; Brennan joins and they perform together.
jokes.punchline: The crowd's complete 180 — from 'get off the stage, you dick' to full participatory dancing — is an absurdist triumph that the film earns through sheer commitment. By 90:43 the mixer has been converted.
jokes.explanation: The cumulative payoff of the entire Boats and Hoes arc. The impact is high because it earns its absurdism — a genuinely cathartic crowd reversal triggered by an objectively terrible song performed by two 40-year-old men-children. The film commits fully and the audience rewards it.

jokes.text: Derek, in tears: 'You did it, Derek. I made a kite fly.'
jokes.setup: The performance has been a massive success; Derek is emotionally overwhelmed.
jokes.punchline: Derek congratulates himself in the third person — 'You did it, Derek' — and his metaphor for his achievement is 'I made a kite fly.' The narcissistic self-credit after Brennan and Dale did everything, plus the bathos of 'made a kite fly' as his self-image, is perfect Derek.
jokes.explanation: Adam Scott's Derek is the film's most consistent comedy engine. 'You did it, Derek. I made a kite fly.' — self-congratulation in the third person for other people's work, using a metaphor that is both grandiose and strangely humble — is excellent character comedy. 'Made a kite fly' is a weirdly specific, perfectly chosen image of modest triumph that Derek has somehow inflated into personal mythology.

jokes.text: Brennan: 'You're the best big brother ever!' — said to Dale, who is not his brother (or rather, is his step-brother).
jokes.setup: The performance has ended in triumph; emotional reconciliation is in the air.
jokes.punchline: Brennan's earnest 'best big brother ever' to Dale — after the entire film has been spent on them hating each other, then bonding — lands as genuine emotion delivered in the register of two overgrown children. The film earns this sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Earns its sentiment through the film's commitment. The joke is partly that Brennan means it completely — after everything — and says it with a child's total sincerity.

jokes.text: In the crowd, an older man shouts to someone on a phone: 'I traveled 500 miles to give you my seed. Lumberjack!'
jokes.setup: The triumphant aftermath of the Boats and Hoes performance; party guests mill about.
jokes.punchline: A completely unexplained non-sequitur from a background character — 'I traveled 500 miles to give you my seed. Lumberjack!' — has no context, no payoff, and no explanation. Pure chaos injection.
jokes.explanation: Classic McKay chaos gag — an inexplicable background moment that rewards rewatchers. The low structure score reflects that it's purely random rather than constructed. Impact is decent because of sheer surprise. 'Lumberjack!' as a disconnected exclamation is the kind of line that gets clipped and shared.

jokes.text: 'We're Prestige Worldwide!' / 'Prestige Worldwide!' / 'Fucking Catalina Wine Mixer.' — Brennan and Dale triumphant.
jokes.setup: The performance has succeeded; emotional peak of the sequence.
jokes.punchline: Their victory cry is 'Prestige Worldwide' — their absurd business name — and then 'Fucking Catalina Wine Mixer,' which has been the film's recurring totem of achievement. The full callback lands.
jokes.explanation: Pure payoff moment. The triple callback (Prestige Worldwide, Catalina Wine Mixer) hits because it's the culmination of running threads. 'Fucking Catalina Wine Mixer' said with reverence by multiple characters is perfectly absurd.

jokes.text: Derek to Brennan: 'Look, I'm not great at this Hallmark stuff, but Brennan, when I look at you now... I don't wanna kick you in the head quite as much.'
jokes.setup: Derek is attempting a sincere moment of brotherly reconciliation.
jokes.punchline: 'I don't wanna kick you in the head quite as much' as his heartfelt expression of affection is a perfect Derek line — the bar is 'less desire to inflict cranial violence,' and he's presenting this as a Hallmark sentiment.
jokes.explanation: Among the best lines in the reel. The structure is perfect: 'I'm not great at this Hallmark stuff' primes us for a sincere emotion, and 'I don't wanna kick you in the head quite as much' is the most Derek possible payoff. The qualifier 'quite as much' — not 'at all,' just 'quite as much' — is a master touch. Economy is near-perfect. This is legitimately an 8+ joke by the calibration standard.

jokes.text: On the topic of hugging: 'Yeah, you'd like that, faggot. Sorry. I'm...' — Derek immediately retreating into defensiveness after almost hugging Brennan.
jokes.setup: Robert suggests the brothers could hug; a moment of genuine connection seems possible.
jokes.punchline: Derek's reflex homophobic deflection — 'Yeah, you'd like that, faggot' — immediately followed by 'Sorry. I'm...' (incomplete apology, recognizing he went too far) is a character collapse caught in real time.
jokes.explanation: The 'Sorry. I'm...' incomplete retraction is the best part — Derek catching himself mid-slur and being unable to complete the apology is a sharp character beat. The slur itself is dated but the structural observation (alpha-male emotional incapacity in real time) is well-executed.

jokes.text: Robert assessing the near-hug: 'Gotten close to a hug.'
jokes.setup: The attempted hug has dissolved into awkwardness and a homophobic slur.
jokes.punchline: Robert's diplomatic summary — 'gotten close to a hug' — treats the failed attempt as a measurable step toward progress, like a golf handicap improvement.
jokes.explanation: Robert's compulsive positivity reframing a failed hug as incremental progress is a good button on the sequence. 'Gotten close to a hug' as a formal assessment is funny in its specificity.

jokes.text: Brennan introduces Denise as his 'girlfriend'; Denise immediately corrects: 'Actually, I'm his therapist. We are in absolutely no way dating.'
jokes.setup: Brennan introduces Denise to the family with pride, implying a romantic relationship.
jokes.punchline: Denise's clinical, emphatic correction — 'we are in absolutely no way dating' — delivered to the whole family group, is a sharp deflation and also implies Brennan has been misrepresenting the relationship.
jokes.explanation: Clean setup/punchline with strong escalation potential. 'We are in absolutely no way dating' — the 'absolutely no way' emphasis is perfect — implies Brennan has been introducing her as his girlfriend to everyone, which is both sad and funny. Good economy.

jokes.text: Denise: 'Brennan told me he was going to hurl his body off a helicopter into shark-infested waters, so I had a legal obligation to be here.'
jokes.setup: Denise has explained she's Brennan's therapist, not his girlfriend.
jokes.punchline: Her reason for attending — legal obligation due to patient suicidal ideation involving shark-infested helicopter jumping — reframes the entire Catalina Wine Mixer sequence as a therapist's emergency intervention.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'hurl his body off a helicopter into shark-infested waters' as the described threat is very funny — it's not generic suicidal ideation, it's an extremely specific, almost adventure-movie scenario. Recontextualizes Brennan's bravery speech as a clinical emergency.

jokes.text: Robert to Denise: 'Don't wanna appear too eager, and that is a good strategy too.' — interpreting her professional distance as romantic coyness.
jokes.setup: Denise has made absolutely clear she is Brennan's therapist and they are not dating.
jokes.punchline: Robert wilfully misreads her clinical boundaries as flirtatious playing-hard-to-get, coaching Brennan on her 'strategy.' His obliviousness is complete and sincere.
jokes.explanation: Robert's incorrigible optimism about Brennan's romantic prospects — reading a therapist's professional ethics as romantic strategy — is a good beat. His 'That is a good strategy too' treats the situation as a chess game Denise is winning.

jokes.text: Denise's clinical compliment to Brennan: '...in strictly the most clinical and professional sense possible, with no emotional, intimate, sexual, or any other undertones that you could possibly infer.'
jokes.setup: Denise has said Brennan was 'incredibly brave' — a warm compliment.
jokes.punchline: She then exhaustively qualifies it, adding disclaimer after disclaimer until the compliment is stripped of all human warmth. The escalation of qualifiers — emotional, intimate, sexual, 'any other undertones you could possibly infer' — is funny through accumulation.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the comprehensiveness of the disclaimer — Denise has thought through every possible misinterpretation and pre-emptively denied it, which suggests she knows exactly what Brennan will infer and is trying desperately to prevent it. Slight demerit for running a beat long.

jokes.text: Robert, confused, asks: 'What poem is that from? Is that James Joyce?'
jokes.setup: Denise has just delivered a clinical therapist's disclaimer about the lack of emotional undertones.
jokes.punchline: Robert, apparently deeply moved by what he heard, tries to identify it as literature — specifically James Joyce — revealing that he found it poetic even though it was a legal disclaimer.
jokes.explanation: 'Is that James Joyce?' is a perfectly economical button — Robert's sincere misidentification of therapeutic boilerplate as great literature is funny on multiple levels. His cultural reference (Joyce specifically, not just 'a poem') adds a layer of misplaced sophistication.

jokes.text: Alice tells Dale: 'I like making sex with you. I do. But you're also married. It's over.'
jokes.setup: Alice and Dale have apparently been having an affair (Alice is married to Brennan's boss Derek).
jokes.punchline: 'I like making sex with you' — not 'having sex,' but 'making sex' — is an odd, slightly off-register phrasing that combined with the matter-of-fact breakup delivery creates an uncomfortable deadpan comedy beat.
jokes.explanation: 'Making sex' is a mild comedy touch — slightly off phrasing that lands as an accidental malapropism or a character voice choice. The scene is more plot than comedy.

jokes.text: Dale spots Alice leaving and falls to his knees dramatically: 'Please don't leave me.' Alice: 'Oh, my God. Look at that whale.' Dale: 'Where?'
jokes.setup: Dale is emotionally devastated by Alice ending the affair; he's on his knees begging.
jokes.punchline: Alice shouts 'Look at that whale' — Dale, instantaneously, forgets his heartbreak and says 'Where?' His childlike distraction response — a whale has completely overridden his grief — is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel and possibly the film. The structure is flawless: Dale at peak emotional devastation, on his knees, 'Please don't leave me' — then a single word ('whale') and he's completely gone. 'Where?' with the implied physical pivot toward the ocean is perfect character comedy AND perfect structure. Dale's attention span overriding his heartbreak in under two seconds is the film's thesis statement about these characters in miniature. The economy (one word trigger, one word response) is near-perfect. Comparable to the top-tier anchor examples.

jokes.text: Derek's story: 'So I was with Seal... we were just taking a chopper up to Everest base camp, and the plot to my Sherpa...' — immediately interrupted.
jokes.setup: Post-triumph, Derek is in storytelling mode.
jokes.punchline: Derek's casual opener — 'I was with Seal' (the singer), on a helicopter to Everest — establishes Derek's brand of name-dropping, adventure-bragging absurdism. He can't even finish the sentence before being cut off, which is itself the joke.
jokes.explanation: Derek's incorrigible need to tell impossibly glamorous anecdotes (Seal, Everest, Sherpa) even in this moment is a good character beat. The interruption before the punchline is the joke — the story doesn't need to end.

jokes.text: Brennan explains the new business: 'Most karaoke it's, Open to everyone. Hey, just get up and have fun. Not you guys. If you can't sing, just sit down. That's our motto.'
jokes.setup: Robert asks about the karaoke business; Brennan explains their philosophy.
jokes.punchline: Their karaoke business motto — 'If you can't sing, just sit down' — is the antithesis of karaoke's entire purpose. Exclusionary karaoke, run by men who performed 'Boats and Hoes' at a corporate event, is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The irony that Dale and Brennan — who performed a song called 'Boats and Hoes' to a booing corporate crowd — now run an exclusive karaoke bar where bad singers must 'sit down' is a rich character-comedy payoff. 'That's our motto' said with entrepreneurial pride is excellent. 'It's the big leagues' from Dale is a perfect button.

jokes.text: Dale: 'It's the big leagues.'
jokes.setup: Brennan has just explained their karaoke business motto ('if you can't sing, sit down').
jokes.punchline: Dale's solemn confirmation — 'It's the big leagues' — applied to their exclusive karaoke bars, run by two men who once performed 'Boats and Hoes' to a hostile crowd.
jokes.explanation: Four words doing a lot of work. Dale's gravitas about their karaoke empire is funny because of everything we know about these men. Good economy, good character integration.

jokes.text: During the buildup to the surprise: Dale asks 'Did you get me a tiger, Dad?'
jokes.setup: Robert is building anticipation for the Christmas surprise with 'don't peek, be patient.'
jokes.punchline: Dale's guess — a tiger — both establishes his childlike expectation scale and is funnier than any reasonable guess would be.
jokes.explanation: One word (tiger) does a lot of character work — Dale, apparently, believes a tiger is on the gift table as a reasonable possibility. Good economy, strong character integration.

jokes.text: Robert gives a 'Christmas surprise' — he's put the boat in a tree.
jokes.setup: Robert announces a Christmas surprise and builds anticipation with 'don't peek' and 'be patient.'
jokes.punchline: He has mounted the boat — The Gilded Lady — in a tree as a Christmas gift. This is an absurdist escalation from the film's earlier boat-related chaos.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of the boat in the tree is a strong visual payoff — Robert has done the most elaborate, most absurd possible version of the gift. 'Dad, I can't believe you put the boat in the tree!' is delivered with appropriate awe. 'She lives!' The callback to the Gilded Lady from the earlier boat-sinking sequence makes this land harder.

jokes.text: Robert opens the crate to reveal pirate hats — Brennan and Dale: 'Pirate hats! Pirate hats!'
jokes.setup: The boat is in the tree; now Robert keeps revealing additional gifts.
jokes.punchline: The parade of increasingly unhinged gifts — pirate hats, then hustlers (card dealers?), then crossbows, then Chewbacca masks — escalates to absurdity while Brennan and Dale respond with identical ecstatic enthusiasm for each item.
jokes.explanation: The escalating gift reveal — pirate hats → hustlers → crossbows → Chewbacca masks — works through accumulation and the men's complete equality of enthusiasm for each item. No gift is more exciting than any other; all are met with the identical ecstatic echo. The rhythm of 'X!' / 'X!' is a perfectly calibrated comedy structure.

jokes.text: Robert: 'But Brennan sure can wear the shit out of that pirate hat.'
jokes.setup: Robert has just conceded the whole situation is 'completely fucked up.'
jokes.punchline: His pivot to genuine paternal pride about Brennan's pirate hat style — 'sure can wear the shit out of that pirate hat' — treats pirate hat-wearing aptitude as a legitimate parental boast.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the gift sequence. 'Brennan sure can wear the shit out of that pirate hat' is sincere paternal pride applied to a pirate hat — the specificity of the compliment (not just wearing it, but wearing the shit out of it) is the extra craft touch. Richard Jenkins's delivery would make this land hard.

jokes.text: Chewbacca masks revealed: 'Chewbacca masks! Chewbacca masks!' — then Dale: 'It's okay that mine's not movie-quality.'
jokes.setup: The gift escalation continues with Chewbacca masks as the final item.
jokes.punchline: Dale's only note — genuinely unbothered — is to acknowledge that his Chewbacca mask is not movie-quality. His total equanimity about receiving an inferior Halloween-store Chewbacca mask as a grown adult is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Dale's single qualifier — 'it's okay that mine's not movie-quality' — reveals that his Chewbacca standards are specific (he knows what movie-quality looks like), and that he's made peace with the downgrade. His complete lack of complaint despite the clearly noted inferiority is excellent character comedy.

jokes.text: Gardocki (bully from earlier in the film) appears and says: 'Well, if it isn't Dale Doback and his little butt buddy.'
jokes.setup: Brennan and Dale are outside; a figure from their past appears.
jokes.punchline: Gardocki's reappearance — using the same kind of juvenile taunting language from earlier in the film — sets up the revenge sequence. The term 'butt buddy' from a grown adult is itself a character comedy beat.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the revenge beat that follows. Mildly funny as a character type but not notable in isolation.

jokes.text: Brennan's response: 'Sticks and stones may break my bones... but I'm gonna kick you repeatedly in the balls, Gardocki!'
jokes.setup: Gardocki has insulted them; Brennan begins with the nursery rhyme 'sticks and stones may break my bones but words will never hurt me' — implying a mature, dismissive response.
jokes.punchline: He pivots mid-rhyme to 'I'm gonna kick you repeatedly in the balls, Gardocki!' — subverting the pacifist nursery rhyme with a very specific, violent threat.
jokes.explanation: Perfect misdirection structure. 'Sticks and stones may break my bones' is one of the most familiar pacifist phrases in the language — the setup is completely committed to it, and the pivot to 'I'm gonna kick you REPEATEDLY in the balls, Gardocki!' is a very funny subversion. The word 'repeatedly' is crucial — not once, but repeatedly. And 'Gardocki!' as the button (his surname, formal and furious) adds the final touch. Among the reel's best-structured jokes.

jokes.text: Brennan forces Gardocki to look at white dog feces and says: 'Your actions have consequences! When you oppress people, they rise up in a fiery anger!'
jokes.setup: Brennan and Dale have apparently overpowered Gardocki and his crew during the fight scene.
jokes.punchline: Brennan delivers a speech about oppression and consequences while forcing Gardocki to look at dog poop. The grandiosity of the rhetoric ('fiery anger,' 'oppress people') applied to a neighborhood bully dispute with dog feces as the visual aid is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Brennan's tendency to frame mundane events in the grandest possible political terms ('oppress,' 'fiery anger') while pointing at dog excrement is very much in character. 'Do you see it?!' adds to the absurd seriousness.

jokes.text: Brennan dismisses Gardocki: 'We're not like you. We're grown-ups, motherfucker!' — then immediately: 'Say hi to your dad. We went to high school together.'
jokes.setup: Brennan has just finished the oppression speech and is dismissing the bullies.
jokes.punchline: 'We're grown-ups, motherfucker!' — the declaration of maturity punctuated with 'motherfucker' — immediately followed by a neighborly 'Say hi to your dad, we went to high school together,' delivered with complete tonal whiplash.
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best lines. 'We're grown-ups, motherfucker!' is already funny as a self-defeating assertion of maturity (swearing while claiming adult status), but the immediate pivot to 'Say hi to your dad, we went to high school together' — going from maximum aggression to neighborly small talk in one breath — is a masterclass in tonal whiplash. The casualness of the second line, as if completing a normal interaction, is what makes it exceptional. High quotability.

jokes.text: Post-fight, the cops arrive. Brennan: 'I guess this is what it feels like to be grown up.'
jokes.setup: Brennan and Dale have just beaten up a group of bullies; police sirens are heard.
jokes.punchline: Brennan's conclusion — sitting in the aftermath of a brawl with the police coming — that 'this is what it feels like to be grown up' is the film's thesis in ironic miniature. This is their version of adulthood.
jokes.explanation: Perfect ironic button on the bully sequence. 'I guess this is what it feels like to be grown up' — said with genuine satisfaction, sitting in the ruins of a street brawl — is both a character statement and a thematic joke. Brennan's sincere pride in this as adulthood is the film's central irony crystallized.

jokes.text: Dale asks Brennan if he touched his drum set years ago; insists he won't get mad; Brennan insists he didn't do it. Dale: 'Then I owe you an apology.' Brennan: 'No, you don't, at all.' Dale: 'Why wouldn't you take an apology if you didn't do it?' Brennan: 'Just because I'm cool. It doesn't matter.'
jokes.setup: Dale returns to the original conflict of the film — whether Brennan touched his drum set — in a moment of post-victory emotional settling.
jokes.punchline: The callback to the film's inciting incident (the drum set) in this tender moment is funny, but Brennan's refusal to accept an apology he is due — 'just because I'm cool, it doesn't matter' — is the richer joke. His casual martyrdom (refusing vindication as a flex) is a perfect character capstone.
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully constructed callback to the film's very beginning. The structure — Dale apologizing, Brennan refusing the apology, Dale logically pointing out this makes no sense, Brennan's inexplicable 'just because I'm cool' — is an earned character comedy moment. 'It doesn't matter' as the final word, delivered with zero irony, is both funny and oddly touching as a statement of their friendship. Among the reel's strongest jokes.
